# Tutorial Overview {#sec-overview}

This tutorial is a step-by-step walk-through of the open-source analog mixed-signal (AMS) chip flow based on the [`ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template) repository for the ihp-sg13g2 130nm Open-PDK. It covers:

- [Overview](#sec-overview) and [Installation](#sec-installation) of [IIC-OSIC-TOOLS](https://github.com/iic-jku/IIC-OSIC-TOOLS)
- [Digital macro design](#sec-digital)
  - Design files written in SystemVerilog
  - Linting with [Verilator](https://github.com/verilator/verilator)
  - Simulation with [Icarus Verilog](https://github.com/steveicarus/iverilog) and [cocotb](https://github.com/cocotb/cocotb)
  - Viewing waveforms with [GTKWave](https://github.com/gtkwave/gtkwave) and [Surfer](https://gitlab.com/surfer-project/surfer)
  - Synthesis, placement, routing, and verification with [Yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys), [OpenROAD](https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD), and [LibreLane](https://github.com/librelane/librelane)
  - Logic equivalence check of the netlist against the RTL with [EQY](https://github.com/YosysHQ/eqy)
- [Analog macro design](#sec-analog)
  - Schematic entry in [Xschem](https://github.com/StefanSchippers/xschem)
  - Simulation with [Ngspice](https://github.com/danchitnis/ngspice-sf-mirror) and [VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK)
  - Monte Carlo / mismatch characterisation with [CACE](https://github.com/fossi-foundation/cace)
  - Layout in [KLayout](https://github.com/KLayout/klayout)
  - Verification with DRC, LVS, PEX using [KLayout](https://github.com/KLayout/klayout), [Magic](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/magic) + [Netgen](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/netgen), plus [gdscheck](https://github.com/aesc-silicon/gdscheck) as a third DRC engine
- [RF macro design](#sec-rf)
  - Layouts written as KLayout Python scripts, and programmatic layouts with [GDSFactory](https://github.com/gdsfactory/gdsfactory)
  - EM simulation of RF passives with [AWS Palace](https://github.com/awslabs/palace) and [gds2palace](https://github.com/VolkerMuehlhaus/gds2palace_ihp_sg13g2)
  - Lumped-element models of the EM results with [snp2le](https://github.com/iic-jku/snp2le)
  - Large-signal RF simulation (PSS, PNOISE, PAC, ACSP) with [VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK) and a post-layout simulation at 20 GHz
- [Top-level assembly and padframe generation](#sec-top) with logos and fill structures using SystemVerilog and the [LibreLane](https://github.com/librelane/librelane) flow.
- [Starting your own chip](#sec-new-chip) from the template with a single `make project` target.

The example design used throughout the tutorial contains:

- Two digital `counter_top` macros (8-bit synchronous up-counters)
- Two `inverter_top` macros, one used as a 4-channel CMOS digital inverter, one as a 2-channel analog inverter
- One `RM_IHPSG13_1P_1024x32_c2_bm_bist` single-port SRAM macro
- A 32-pad padframe (8 pads per side) with I/O, power, analog, and bidirectional pads
- The top-level chip assembly with power distribution network (PDN), logos, and fill structures

The tutorial ends with a set of exercises that apply the same flow to a modified counter, a ring oscillator using the inverters, a modified top-level floorplan and pinout, and the counter on another standard cell library. This way, all important steps of the flow are covered in a hands-on manner.

::: {.callout-tip}
The tutorial can be used both for self-study and as the basis for a workshop. Each section can be followed independently.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
After the tutorial, readers should be able to use the template repository for custom silicon projects and understand how to apply the open-source tools in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container to design, simulate, build, and verify AMS chips with the ihp-sg13g2 Open-PDK.
:::

# Tools {#sec-tools}

Numerous open-source chip design tools cover the entire development workflow for purely digital, purely analog, or mixed analog-digital chips. Managing these many tools regarding installation, updates, and maintenance is complex, especially given the rapid pace of change. Therefore, the [Institute for Integrated Circuits and Quantum Computing](https://www.jku.at/en/institute-for-integrated-circuits-and-quantum-computing/) at [Johannes Kepler University](https://www.jku.at/) (JKU) Linz, Austria, decided to build an all-in-one Docker container ([IIC-OSIC-TOOLS](https://github.com/iic-jku/IIC-OSIC-TOOLS)) that is updated monthly and supports all essential tools and PDKs. This eliminates the need for the time-consuming individual installation of many tools, and a reproducible development environment (important for reproducing past tapeouts) is available within a GNU/Linux-based virtual machine.

## IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Overview

@fig-tools-overview shows a rough overview of the most important tools in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container. Additional tools are also included, which are documented on the associated [GitHub page](https://github.com/iic-jku/IIC-OSIC-TOOLS).
The open-source AMS flow used in this tutorial relies on several tools, namely [Xschem](https://github.com/StefanSchippers/xschem), [Magic](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/magic), [Netgen](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/netgen), [KLayout](https://github.com/KLayout/klayout), [Ngspice](https://github.com/danchitnis/ngspice-sf-mirror), [VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK), [CACE](https://github.com/fossi-foundation/cace), [LibreLane](https://github.com/librelane/librelane), [Yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys), [EQY](https://github.com/YosysHQ/eqy), [OpenROAD](https://github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenROAD), [Verilator](https://github.com/verilator/verilator), [cocotb](https://github.com/cocotb/cocotb), [GTKWave](https://github.com/gtkwave/gtkwave), and [Surfer](https://gitlab.com/surfer-project/surfer).
The container also ships with four PDKs: [SkyWater sky130A](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/open_pdks), [GlobalFoundries gf180mcuD](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/open_pdks), [IHP ihp-sg13cmos5l](https://github.com/IHP-GmbH/ihp-sg13cmos5l) and [IHP ihp-sg13g2](https://github.com/IHP-GmbH/IHP-Open-PDK) used by this template.

## PDK Selection {#sec-pdk}

As mentioned above, the container includes four Open-PDKs. To activate or switch the active PDK, the following two options are available. More detailed instructions can be found in the container's [`README.md`](https://github.com/iic-jku/IIC-OSIC-TOOLS/blob/main/README.md#2-installed-pdks).

1. **`.designinit` file:** Copy the [`.designinit`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/.designinit) file referencing the ihp-sg13g2 PDK into your `designs/` directory and restart the container. The PDK is then picked automatically every time the container is launched in that directory.

2. **On-the-fly switch:** Run

   ```sh
   sak-pdk ihp-sg13g2
   ```

   inside the container. This switches the active PDK for the current session without modifying any file. When called without arguments (`sak-pdk`), a list of installed PDKs is shown.

::: {.callout-tip}
By default, the container is already configured for `ihp-sg13g2`, so both options above are only needed when switching between PDKs. However, since this tutorial can also be used for all other PDKs, it is worth knowing how to switch the active PDK.
:::

Every `Makefile` in this repository guards against a mismatch. All targets except `help` and `clean` (plus `clean-all` at the top level) compare `$PDK` against `REQUIRED_PDK`, which defaults to `ihp-sg13g2`, and abort before any tool starts:

```sh
sak-pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l
make librelane
```

```text
Makefile:27: *** PDK is "ihp-sg13cmos5l", but this chip needs "ihp-sg13g2". Run `sak-pdk ihp-sg13g2` in this shell and retry, or pass REQUIRED_PDK= to skip this check.  Stop.
```

The check is a parse-time conditional at the top of each `Makefile`, not a prerequisite of each target, so it costs nothing and cannot be forgotten when a target is added. Without it a wrong PDK mixes technologies silently: LibreLane hardens against the wrong tech LEF and standard cells, DRC and LVS run against the wrong rule deck, Magic reads the wrong `magicrc`, and the results still look valid.

Since this tutorial can also be followed with another PDK, the expected PDK is a variable. Override it, or switch the check off entirely:

```sh
make <target> REQUIRED_PDK=<pdk>     # require a different PDK
make <target> REQUIRED_PDK=          # skip the check
```

# Repository Overview {#sec-repo}

## Purpose

This Makefile-driven repository simulates, builds, and fully verifies (DRC, LVS, PEX) a complete analog mixed-signal chip for the ihp-sg13g2 130nm Open-PDK, including padframe generation and top-level assembly. It uses:

- [**LibreLane**](https://github.com/librelane/librelane) for digital macro hardening, padframe generation and top-level assembly
- [**Xschem**](https://github.com/StefanSchippers/xschem) for schematic entry
- [**Ngspice**](https://github.com/danchitnis/ngspice-sf-mirror), [**VACASK**](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK) and [**CACE**](https://github.com/fossi-foundation/cace) for analog simulation
- [**KLayout**](https://github.com/KLayout/klayout) for viewing and routing of the layout
- [**Magic**](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/magic) + [**Netgen**](https://github.com/rtimothyedwards/netgen) and [**KLayout**](https://github.com/KLayout/klayout) for DRC, LVS and PEX verification
- [**gdscheck**](https://github.com/aesc-silicon/gdscheck) as a third, standalone DRC engine with its own rule decks
- [**AWS Palace**](https://github.com/awslabs/palace), [**gds2palace**](https://github.com/VolkerMuehlhaus/gds2palace_ihp_sg13g2) and [**snp2le**](https://github.com/iic-jku/snp2le) for the EM simulation of RF passives and their lumped-element models
- **SystemVerilog**, [**cocotb**](https://github.com/cocotb/cocotb), [**GTKWave**](https://github.com/gtkwave/gtkwave) and [**Surfer**](https://gitlab.com/surfer-project/surfer) for digital simulation

The repository is the starting point for your own custom silicon and provides a universal design flow solution: Just clone the repo, enter the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container, and run `make all` to get a tapeout-ready analog mixed-signal chip. Focus on your design and do not worry about the tools and the design flow!

Furthermore, it serves as a regression test for the above-mentioned open-source tools and their dependencies using the ihp-sg13g2 Open-PDK.

## Examples

Examples based on this template are:

- [TinyWhisper](https://github.com/iic-jku/TinyWhisper): An Open-Source Fully-Integrated Multi-Mode Short-Wave Transmitter for Amateur Radio Applications in 130-nm CMOS
- [SPARX](https://github.com/iic-jku/SG13CMOS_SPARX): An Open-Source, Automated, Programmatically Generated, Frequency-Scalable Six-Port Receiver in 130-nm CMOS
- [Multi-Project Chip](https://github.com/iic-jku/gf180mcu-jku-projects) for the wafer.space gf180mcuD MPW run

| [`netlist/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/netlist/) | Synthesis, schematic, layout, and PEX netlists used for top-level LVS and simulation. |
| [`packaging/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/packaging/) | Automated bondplan generation: config, flow script, package and bondplan GDS, bonding diagrams, and bond report (see @sec-packaging). |
| [`release/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/release/) | Tapeout submission artifacts grouped by version. |

## Workflow

The flow is driven by Makefiles. After cloning the repository and entering the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container, every step is invoked via a `make` target. The default target of every `Makefile` is `help`, so `make` (without arguments) prints the list of available targets. Every `Makefile` checks the active PDK first and stops on a mismatch, see @sec-pdk. After entering the container, the starting folder is `/foss/designs/`.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template.git
cd ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template
make help              # show available targets at the top level
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Instead of `git clone`, you can start by clicking the green "Use this template" button on the GitHub page to create your own copy of the repository. This way, you can push your changes to your own GitHub repository and even make it public if you want to share your custom silicon design with the community. When the copy is to become your own chip, `make project NAME=<name>` renames it and removes the template-only content, see @sec-new-chip.
:::

To find and open a design file, run `make open` in the container's VNC/noVNC desktop. It shows one button per design file of the folder, grouped by directory, and a click opens the file in its tool: Xschem for `.sch` and `.sym`, KLayout for `.gds`, GTKWave for waveforms and gvim for RTL, scripts and configs. The checkboxes select the file types, and the filter field keeps only the paths that contain the typed text. @fig-make-open shows the top level with only the schematics and symbols selected. The window is rescanned every 15 s, so files a running flow writes appear on their own. The [top-level README](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/README.md#open-the-design-files) lists every file type and option.

![`make open` at the top level after `None` and ticking `.sch` and `.sym`: all 18 schematics and symbols of the chip and both macros, each one click away from Xschem.](fig/make_open/make_open.png){#fig-make-open}

Each macro under [`macros/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/) has its own `Makefile` and `README.md`, including macro-specific targets. These targets are invoked by the top-level build flow, but you can also run them directly from inside each macro folder. @fig-targets-overview shows how the Makefile targets across the repository are connected.

The colour scheme groups targets by the final deliverable they produce, so beginners can follow one colour from `make all` to the generated outputs:

- **Orange (top chip / main)**: This branch includes `make all` and all targets that contribute to the top-level chip GDS. In the `build-top` chain of the [top-level Makefile](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/Makefile), these are `librelane-nodrc`, `copy-*`, `add-logo-fill`, and `render-gds`.
- **Yellow (bondpad IP)**: This branch includes `build-bondpad` and all targets inside [`ip/sg13g2_ip__bondpad_70x70/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/ip/sg13g2_ip__bondpad_70x70/).
- **Teal (RF pad IP)**: This branch includes `build-rfpad` and all targets inside [`ip/sg13g2_ip__rfpad_70x70/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/ip/sg13g2_ip__rfpad_70x70/).
- **Purple (logos IP)**: This branch includes `build-logos` and the two sub-Makefiles under [`ip/sg13g2_ip__jku/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/ip/sg13g2_ip__jku/) and [`ip/sg13g2_ip__jku_names/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/ip/sg13g2_ip__jku_names/).
- **Blue (digital macro)**: This branch includes `build-counter` and the [`macros/counter/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/) Makefile.
- **Green (analog macro)**: This branch includes `build-inverter` and the [`macros/inverter/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/) Makefile.
- **Red (packaging)**: This branch includes `bondplan` and the automated bondplan flow in [`packaging/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/packaging/) (see @sec-packaging).
- **Grey (simulation and verification)**: This branch includes intermediate targets that feed the coloured deliverables (`sim-all`, `build-all`, `build-macros`, `init-submodules`, `sim-*-cocotb`).

Solid arrows represent direct `$(MAKE) <target>` calls within a single Makefile. Dashed arrows represent calls that descend into a subdirectory: recursive `$(MAKE) -C <dir> all` calls into a sub-Makefile (one per coloured deliverable), or the Python bondplan flow in `packaging/`. The numbers on the second level indicate the execution order of `make all` (build, verify, simulate, package), and the vertical order inside the coloured boxes reflects the execution order of each sub-Makefile's `all` target.

![Overview of the Makefile targets that `make all` resolves to. Every coloured branch corresponds to one deliverable (top chip, bondpad, RF pad, logos, digital macro, analog macro, packaging). The grey targets connect `make all` to those branches.](fig/targets_overview/targets_overview.svg){#fig-targets-overview}

# Digital Macro Implementation {#sec-digital}

The [`counter`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/) macro is the digital reference macro of the template. It is a parameterisable synchronous up-counter with synchronous active-high reset implemented with SystemVerilog in [`counter.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/rtl/counter.sv). The top-level wrapper [`counter_top.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/rtl/counter_top.sv) converts the chip's active-low reset to an active-high signal. The default width is 8 bits, so the counter wraps from 255 back to 0.

## Directory Structure

The counter design files are located in [`macros/counter/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/), and the relevant folders are:

| [`testbenches/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/testbenches/) | `verilog/`, `cocotb/`, and `xschem/` testbenches with pre-configured GTKWave and Surfer view files. |
| [`flow/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/flow/)           | LibreLane configuration (`config.yaml`, `pin_order.cfg`, `impl.sdc`, `signoff.sdc`). |

## Reading the RTL

The macro is split into a parameterised counter and a top-level wrapper that converts the chip's active-low reset to the internal active-high reset of the counter.

### `counter.sv`

The logic is implemented in [`counter.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/rtl/counter.sv). It is an $N$-bit synchronous up-counter with reset and enable, and it wraps at `CTR_MAX`. $N$ defaults to 8, so the counter counts from 0 to 255 and then wraps back to 0.

```{.systemverilog filename="macros/counter/rtl/counter.sv"}
{{< include ../macros/counter/rtl/counter.sv >}}
```

### `counter_top.sv`

[`counter_top.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/rtl/counter_top.sv) wraps the counter and converts the active-low reset (`reset_n_i`) to an active-high signal `reset`.

```{.systemverilog filename="macros/counter/rtl/counter_top.sv"}
{{< include ../macros/counter/rtl/counter_top.sv >}}
```

Shared defaults are defined in [`constants.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/rtl/constants.sv). For example, for the final implementation, the maximum counter value is defined in `constants.sv` with the variable `COUNTER_MAX_DEFAULT`. For the testbenches, `CLK_FREQ_DEFAULT` is defined there to set the default clock frequency (e.g. 50 MHz) for the simulations. They are exposed as `` `define `` macros instead of a SystemVerilog `package`, because Yosys 0.64 cannot parse `import pkg::*` in a module header.

::: {.callout-note}
Open the three RTL files (using `gedit` or `vim`), follow and understand the counter through reset, hold, increment, and wrap-around.
:::

## Linting

[Linting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lint_(software)) is done with [Verilator](https://www.veripool.org/verilator/) and can be executed with the following commands.

```sh
cd macros/counter
make lint-verilog                # lint the full counter_top design
make lint-verilog CELL=counter   # lint only the standalone counter
make lint-verilog-all            # lint counter and counter_top in sequence
```

`make lint-verilog-all` is also the lint step called by `make all`.

## Simulation

### RTL with SystemVerilog testbench (Icarus Verilog)

A SystemVerilog testbench ([`counter_top_tb.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/testbenches/verilog/counter_top_tb.sv)) checks reset, hold, increment, and wrap-around. Run it with the following commands.

```sh
make sim-rtl-verilog
make sim-view-verilog               # open in GTKWave (default)
make sim-view-verilog WAVEFORM_VIEWER=surfer
```

![RTL Verilog waveform of `counter_top` in GTKWave.](fig/counter_top/counter_top_verilog_gtkwave.png){#fig-counter-top-verilog-gtkwave}

### RTL and gate-level with cocotb

The [cocotb](https://www.cocotb.org/) testbench ([`counter_top_tb.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/testbenches/cocotb/counter_top_tb.py)) checks the same four cases (reset, hold, increment, and wrap-around) as the SystemVerilog testbench, but implements them in Python.

```sh
make sim-rtl-cocotb                # RTL simulation
make sim-gl-cocotb                 # post-synthesis gate-level simulation
make sim-view-cocotb               # view in GTKWave
make sim-view-cocotb WAVEFORM_VIEWER=surfer
```

![Gate-level cocotb waveform of `counter_top` in GTKWave.](fig/counter_top/counter_top_cocotb_gtkwave.png){#fig-counter-top-cocotb-gtkwave}

The gate-level cocotb run uses the gate-level Verilog netlist produced after synthesis: [`netlist/nl/counter_top.nl.v`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/netlist/nl/). In this tutorial, this netlist for the counter already exists. For new designs, run `make build-top` first to execute the LibreLane flow. It also copies the netlists from the latest LibreLane run back into the source tree with `make copy-netlist`.

## LibreLane Hardening

The LibreLane flow synthesises, places, and routes the macro, runs the verification steps, and writes its final output files to `flow/final/`. The wrapper target `make build-top` runs the flow, renders the final GDS, and copies the reports, final folders, netlists, and render output back into the source tree.

```sh
make build-top
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The macro can also be built as an FPGA bitstream ([`fpga/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/fpga/)) with `make build-fpga`. `counter_top` is synthesised straight onto board pins, without a board-top wrapper, and three boards are supported: pico-ice and iCEBreaker (Lattice iCE40) and ULX3S (Lattice ECP5). Pick one with `make build-fpga` for the default pico-ice, or `make -C fpga BOARD=ulx3s all` for another. IIC-OSIC-TOOLS carries the build chain for all three boards, so the bitstreams build inside the container, and only flashing needs the host, since the container has no USB access. Details are in [`fpga/README.md`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/fpga/README.md). The FPGA flow is not used in this tutorial and is only listed here for reference.
:::

### Sizing the Macro {#sec-hardening-sizing}

Three parameters in [`config.yaml`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/flow/librelane/config.yaml) decide how compact and how fast the hardened macro is.

```{.yaml filename="macros/counter/flow/librelane/config.yaml (code snippet)"}
# Layout / Floorplan Rules
DIE_AREA: [0, 0, 200, 100]
PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT: 40

# Valid values are AREA 0-3 and DELAY 0-4, LibreLane defaults to AREA 0
# DELAY favours speed, AREA favours cell area
# AREA 3 and DELAY 4 always add buffering and gate sizing, so AREA 3 can be larger than AREA 0
SYNTH_STRATEGY: DELAY 4
```

- **`DIE_AREA`** is the macro outline `[x0, y0, x1, y1]` in µm (`FP_SIZING: absolute`). The standard-cell rows fill a core area inside it, which is 188 µm × 68 µm for the counter. The aspect ratio matters as much as the area: the outline has to fit the slot of the macro in the top-level floorplan and leave room for the pins listed in [`pin_order.cfg`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/flow/librelane/pin_order.cfg).
- **`PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT`** is the cell density that global placement aims for. At 40 %, the placer spreads the cells so that most of the core stays free for the clock tree, the buffers added during timing repair, and the routing. The target should stay above the utilisation (cell area divided by free core area), which global placement prints as `Utilization` in its log. A lower target triggers the warning `[GPL-0302] Target density 0.4000 is too low for the available free area`, and global placement then raises the target to the utilisation on its own.
- **`SYNTH_STRATEGY`** selects the ABC script that Yosys uses for logic optimisation and technology mapping. The `AREA 0` to `AREA 3` scripts favour a small cell area, the `DELAY 0` to `DELAY 4` scripts favour short critical paths. `AREA 0` is the LibreLane default. `AREA 3` and `DELAY 4` always add buffering and gate sizing, so in the test runs below, the counter synthesised to 675 µm² with `AREA 0`, 704 µm² with `DELAY 0`, 720 µm² with `AREA 3`, and 742 µm² with `DELAY 4`. The best strategy for a design is found by trying.

No formula gives the right values up front. They are found iteratively. A run of a small macro takes only a few minutes (`make librelane-nodrc` skips the DRC steps), and the following procedure converges within a handful of runs.

1. **Start large and balanced.** Set a generous `DIE_AREA`, several times the cell area that Yosys reports in [`verification/stat.rpt`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/verification/stat.rpt), and a balanced strategy such as `AREA 0` or `DELAY 0`. This run finishes quickly and gives the reference values for cell area, utilisation, and timing slack.
2. **Shrink the die until placement complains.** Reduce `DIE_AREA` step by step and leave `PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT` unchanged. The first complaint is the `[GPL-0302]` warning, which means the die is now too small for the target density. The run can still finish, but shrinking further ends in a hard error, typically `[DPL-0036] Detailed placement failed` once the buffers added by design repair, clock tree synthesis, or timing repair no longer fit.
3. **Step back.** Enlarge the die again until the warning is gone and run the full flow. The result places, routes, and meets timing at the configured density, and it is the starting point for the next step. A denser macro is possible by raising `PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT` on purpose, at the cost of less room for routing and timing repair.
4. **Trade timing slack for area.** Read the worst setup slack in the slowest corner (`nom_slow_1p08V_125C`). If there is margin left, switch to a strategy with a smaller cell area (the `Chip area` line in `*-yosys-synthesis/reports/stat.rpt` of the run) and repeat steps 2 and 3, since a smaller cell area allows a smaller die. If setup fails, move towards `DELAY`, up to `DELAY 4`, or give the placer more room.

Each iteration changes only two values and reads back a few numbers, so the loop can also be scripted or handed to a coding agent. After every run, check the following in the run folder `flow/librelane/runs/<run>/`:

- `warning.log`: the `[GPL-0302]` warning, among others.
- `final/metrics.csv`: `design__instance__utilization`, `timing__setup__ws`, `timing__hold__ws`, and `route__drc_errors`.
- `*-openroad-stapostpnr/summary.rpt`: worst setup and hold slack and the violation counts in all six STA corners. `make copy-reports` copies it to [`verification/stapostpnr_summary.rpt`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/verification/stapostpnr_summary.rpt).

The counter sits far from these limits. In test runs at the configured 200 µm × 100 µm, global placement reported a utilisation of 6.3 % against the target of 40 %, and the worst setup slack was 13.4 ns of the 20 ns clock period. At the same target density, the counter placed without the warning at 100 µm × 60 µm (34 % utilisation), warned but still routed and met timing at 70 µm × 60 µm (52 %), and failed detailed placement at 60 µm × 60 µm (62 %). The runs that finished kept about 13.5 ns of setup slack. With `AREA 0` instead of `DELAY 4`, the 60 µm × 60 µm die routed and met timing as well, which is step 4 at work. Repeating these runs is a good first exercise.

::: {.callout-note}
The configuration sets `GRT_ALLOW_CONGESTION: true`, so global routing continues despite overflow. A die that is too small to route then shows up as detailed routing DRC errors, and the `Checker.TrDRC` step stops the flow.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
A new die size changes the LEF of the macro. Update its placement in the `MACROS` block of the top-level [`config.yaml`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/flow/librelane/config.yaml) and in [`doc/floorplan.md`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/floorplan.md) (see @sec-top). The copy targets take the newest run in `flow/librelane/runs/`, so finish with `make build-top` on the final values.
:::

### Standard Cell Libraries {#sec-hardening-libraries}

The PDK in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container ships three standard cell libraries, and the counter hardens on the first one: the IHP low-voltage library `sg13g2_stdcell` (IHP LV), the IHP high-voltage library `sg13g2_stdcell_hv` (IHP HV), and version 1.1 of [`ez130_8t`](https://iip.ethz.ch/ez-library/ihp130-8t.html) (ETH LV), an [open library from ETH Zurich](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29965) on the same thin-oxide transistors as IHP LV, available since image tag `2026.10`. The following numbers are read from the library views.

| | IHP LV | IHP HV | ETH LV |
|---|---|---|---|
| Library | `sg13g2_stdcell` | `sg13g2_stdcell_hv` | `ez130_8t` |
| Row height | 3.78 µm | 7.14 µm | 3.36 µm |
| Tracks per row at 0.42 µm pitch | 9 | 17 | 8 |
| Site width | 0.48 µm | 0.48 µm | 0.42 µm |
| Transistors | `sg13_lv_*` | `sg13_hv_*` | `sg13_lv_*` |
| Liberty corners | 1.08 V to 1.65 V (6) | 3.0 V to 3.6 V (3) | 1.08 V to 1.32 V (3) |
| Cells in Liberty / LEF | 84 / 84 | 84 / 84 | 214 / 220 |
| Combinational functions | 28 | 28 | 61 |
| Buffer drive strengths | 5 | 5 | 13 |
| Inverter (`inv_1`, `INVX3`) | 5.44 µm² | 13.71 µm² | 4.23 µm² |
| Flip-flop with asynchronous reset (`dfrbpq_1`, `DFFRQX3`) | 48.99 µm² | 147.37 µm² | 28.22 µm² |
| Flip-flop without reset (`DFFQX1`) | none | none | 22.58 µm² |
| Well and substrate ties | in every cell | in every cell | separate `WELLTAP` cell |
| Dynamic power data in Liberty | yes | no | yes |
| Views besides Liberty, LEF, GDS, Verilog, CDL | SPICE, Xschem, VACASK | SPICE, Xschem | none |
| LibreLane configuration in the PDK | yes | yes | no |

So IHP LV is a 9-track library and ETH LV an 8-track library. IHP HV is neither: its thick-oxide cells need 17 tracks. Rows of different height do not abut, so the library is a choice per macro.

Every combinational function of IHP LV also exists in ETH LV, and ETH LV adds 33 more. IHP HV has the same cell set as IHP LV. ETH LV additionally has:

- **Arithmetic:** the full adder `FAX1`, the half adder `HAX2`, the minority gate `MIN3X*`, and the three-input `XOR3X*` and `XNOR3X*`.
- **Multiplexer:** the inverting `MUXI2X*`.
- **Complex gates:** `AO211`, `AO22`, `AO31`, `AOI211`, `AOI31`, `OA21`, `OA211`, `OAI22`, `OAI211`, `OAI221`, `OAI31`, `AOAI211` and `OAOI211`.
- **Gates with inverted inputs:** `AND3B`, `OR3B`, `NAND4B`, `NAND4BB`, `NOR3B`, `NOR4B`, `NOR4BB`, `AOI21B`, `AOI2B1`, `AOI2B2`, `AOI2B2B`, `AOI2BB2`, `OAI2BB2` and `OAI2B2B`.
- **Sequential cells:** the flip-flop without reset `DFFQX*`, the flip-flop banks `DFFRQ2X*` (2 bits) and `DFFRQ4X*` (4 bits, double height) with a shared clock and reset, which the open flow does not infer, and the active-low latch without reset `LATNQX*`.
- **Physical cells:** `WELLTAP`, `FILLER16`, `DECAP16`, `DECAP32`, and the antenna diodes `ANTENNA2`, `ANTENNA4` and `ANTENNA8`.

IHP LV keeps a few cells that ETH LV lacks: the bus keeper `sg13g2_sighold`, the scan flip-flop with set and reset `sg13g2_sdfbbp_1`, and three delay gates against the single `DLY1X2`.

The drive digit is not comparable between the libraries. `BUFX3` has the `max_capacitance` of `sg13g2_buf_1` (0.3 pF), `BUFX12` that of `sg13g2_buf_4` and `BUFX48` that of `sg13g2_buf_16`. A cell with the same drive is smaller by the ratio of the sites, (0.42 × 3.36) / (0.48 × 3.78) = 0.78, and the flip-flops shrink more than that. `INVX1`, `INVX2` and `INVX3` even share one footprint and differ only in transistor width, so a higher digit costs no area but more input capacitance.

The library is selected in [`config.yaml`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/counter/flow/librelane/config.yaml). `STD_CELL_LIBRARY` alone is not enough, because the configuration also names the Liberty files and the corners of IHP LV. For IHP HV, replace the block from `# Define Standard Cells` to `DEFAULT_CORNER` with the following lines. The PDK configuration of the library supplies the rest.

<details>
<summary>Configuration for IHP HV</summary>

```yaml
# Define Standard Cells
STD_CELL_LIBRARY: sg13g2_stdcell_hv

# Technology LIBs
LIB:
  "*_fast_3p60V_m40C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/sg13g2_stdcell_hv/lib/sg13g2_stdcell_hv_fast_3p60V_m40C.lib

  "*_slow_3p00V_125C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/sg13g2_stdcell_hv/lib/sg13g2_stdcell_hv_slow_3p00V_125C.lib

  "*_typ_3p30V_25C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/sg13g2_stdcell_hv/lib/sg13g2_stdcell_hv_typ_3p30V_25C.lib

# Corners
STA_CORNERS:
  - nom_fast_3p60V_m40C
  - nom_slow_3p00V_125C
  - nom_typ_3p30V_25C

DEFAULT_CORNER: nom_typ_3p30V_25C
```

</details>

ETH LV takes more. The image ships its views but no LibreLane configuration, so `STD_CELL_LIBRARY: ez130_8t` stops right away with `no files matched glob pattern .../ez130_8t/lef/sg13g2_tech.lef`. Keep the name of the default library instead and replace everything it implies. Replace the same block with the first of the following two listings, and save the second one as `tracks_ez130.info` next to `config.yaml`.

<details>
<summary>Configuration for ETH LV</summary>

```yaml
# Define Standard Cells
# The name stays at the PDK default, every view it implies is replaced below
STD_CELL_LIBRARY: sg13g2_stdcell

# Views
TECH_LEFS:
  "*": pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/lef/ez130_sg13g2_tech.lef
CELL_LEFS: [pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/lef/ez130_8t.lef]
CELL_GDS: [pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/gds/ez130_8t.gds]
CELL_VERILOG_MODELS: [pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/verilog/ez130_8t.v]
CELL_SPICE_MODELS: [pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/cdl/ez130_8t.cdl]
CELL_CDLS: [pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/cdl/ez130_8t.cdl]
FP_TRACKS_INFO: dir::tracks_ez130.info

# Well and substrate ties
WELLTAP_CELL: WELLTAP
FP_TAPCELL_DIST: 20

# Role cells, matched to the IHP LV defaults on max_capacitance
SYNTH_DRIVING_CELL: BUFX12/Y
SYNTH_CLK_DRIVING_CELL: BUFX12/Y
SYNTH_BUFFER_CELL: BUFX3/A/Y
SYNTH_TIEHI_CELL: TIEHI/Y
SYNTH_TIELO_CELL: TIELO/Y
FILL_CELLS: [FILLER1, FILLER2, FILLER4, FILLER8, FILLER16]
DECAP_CELLS: [DECAP4, DECAP8, DECAP16, DECAP32]
CELL_PAD_EXCLUDE: ["FILLER*", "DECAP*"]
TRISTATE_CELLS: ["TBUFX*", "TINVX*"]
DIODE_CELL: ANTENNA2/A
PDN_RAIL_WIDTH: 0.32
CTS_ROOT_BUFFER: BUFX48
CTS_CLK_BUFFERS: [BUFX24, BUFX12, BUFX6]

# Technology LIBs
LIB:
  "*_fast_1p32V_m40C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/lib/ez130_8t_ff_1p32v_m40c.lib

  "*_slow_1p08V_125C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/lib/ez130_8t_ss_1p08v_125c.lib

  "*_typ_1p20V_25C":
    - pdk_dir::libs.ref/ez130_8t/lib/ez130_8t_tt_1p20v_25c.lib

# Corners
STA_CORNERS:
  - nom_fast_1p32V_m40C
  - nom_slow_1p08V_125C
  - nom_typ_1p20V_25C

DEFAULT_CORNER: nom_typ_1p20V_25C
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Track File for ETH LV</summary>

```text
Metal1 X 0.21 0.42
Metal1 Y 0.0 0.42
Metal2 X 0.21 0.42
Metal2 Y 0.0 0.42
Metal3 X 0.21 0.42
Metal3 Y 0.0 0.42
Metal4 X 0.21 0.42
Metal4 Y 0.0 0.42
Metal5 X 0.21 0.42
Metal5 Y 0.0 0.42
TopMetal1 X 0.0 3.36
TopMetal1 Y 0.0 3.36
TopMetal2 X 0.0 4.0
TopMetal2 Y 0.0 4.0
```

</details>

- `TECH_LEFS`: `ez130_8t` has its own technology LEF with a 0.42 µm vertical routing pitch and the site of 0.42 µm × 3.36 µm. The stock `sg13g2_tech.lef` does not fit the cells.
- `FP_TRACKS_INFO`: the file follows that LEF. With the tracks of the PDK, detailed routing still reports 0 errors, but on the counter Magic then flags 41 and KLayout 5 `M1.b` errors.
- `WELLTAP_CELL`: the cells carry no well and substrate ties. Without tap cells, routing, LVS, antenna and timing stay clean, and only DRC fails: 3914 `LU.a` and `LU.b` errors in Magic and 49 `LU.b` errors in KLayout. With taps every 20 µm the counter gets 103 tap cells (436 µm²).
- `CELL_SPICE_MODELS`: the library ships no SPICE view, so the CDL also serves LVS.
- Role cells: the digit is matched on `max_capacitance`, as explained above. A smaller clock buffer is worth trying, see the bonus of @sec-exercise6.
- Not in the block, since the counter does not need them: `SYNTH_LATCH_MAP` and `SYNTH_TRISTATE_MAP` still name IHP LV cells, so a design with latches or tri-states needs its own maps. `SYNTH_EXCLUDED_CELL_FILE` and `PNR_EXCLUDED_CELL_FILE` still list IHP LV cells, which is harmless apart from the `[STA-0122] cell 'sg13g2_lgcp_1' not found` warnings, but they leave the clock gates and the scan flip-flop of ETH LV selectable.

With these changes `make librelane` runs through on all three libraries with 0 DRC, LVS and antenna errors and timing met. The targets after LibreLane are still written for IHP LV:

| Target | IHP HV | ETH LV |
|---|---|---|
| `make librelane`, `librelane-nodrc` | works | works |
| `make copy-final`, `copy-netlist`, `copy-render`, `render-gds`, `magic-pex` | works | works |
| `make copy-reports`, and with it `make build-top` | stops, it names the six IHP LV corners | stops for the same reason |
| `make generate-xspice` | exits 0 with an empty model, because the recipe names the IHP LV Liberty. With the HV Liberty in the recipe and 3.3 V in the testbench, `make sim-gl-xschem` counts | exits 0 with an empty model, and `spi2xspice.py` cannot read the ETH Liberty yet |
| `make sim-gl-cocotb` | passes with `SCL=sg13g2_stdcell_hv` | fails with `SCL=ez130_8t`: the library has no `sg13g2_udp.v` and no Verilog models for `WELLTAP` and `FILLER*`. It passes after dropping that source and adding empty modules |

::: {.callout-warning}
`make copy-reports` deletes `verification/` before it stops, and `make copy-final` and `make copy-netlist` overwrite committed files. Restore them with `git restore .` in `macros/counter/` after trying another library.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Consequences at the chip top-level

The library of a macro also has consequences at the chip top-level. The template chip runs its core at 1.5 V ([`doc/specifications.md`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/specifications.md)), which is outside the 1.08 V to 1.32 V of ETH LV, so a chip with an ETH LV macro has to run its core at 1.2 V. A test run of the chip with the ETH LV counter routes with 0 errors and LVS matches, where LVS at the chip top-level compares the macro by its pins and its interior is checked in its own LibreLane run. It takes three changes in the top-level [`config.yaml`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/flow/librelane/config.yaml): remove the three corners above 1.32 V from `STA_CORNERS` and from the `lib` list of `counter_top`, set `DEFAULT_CORNER: nom_typ_1p20V_25C`, and add `STA_MACRO_PRIORITIZE_NL: false`, which makes STA read the timing model in `final/lib/` of the macro and not its netlist. Without that line STA finds no Liberty for the ETH LV cells and turns them into black boxes, so all paths through the counter disappear, and only the `Creating black box` lines in `sta.log` give it away. With it, the worst setup slack through a counter is +10.43 ns against +10.50 ns with IHP LV in the same mode, while the worst path of the chip starts at the SRAM and reads +2.30 ns with both. The hold slack from `rst_n_PAD` into `counter2` drops to +0.11 ns against +0.36 ns in the fast corner at 1.32 V. The full-chip DRC was not part of that test. An IHP HV macro needs a 3.3 V domain and level shifters towards the core, which the template chip does not have.
:::

## Viewing the Macro

After the flow finishes, the macro layout can be inspected with KLayout. The container provides the `ke` alias for `klayout -e` (edit mode). With the following command, the final GDS from the latest LibreLane run is opened in KLayout. With the keys `0`, `1`, `2`, ..., `9` you can view different layers as explained in the [KLayout cheatsheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/klayout/klayout_cheatsheet.md) or in the [klayout-layer-shortcuts](https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-layer-shortcuts) plugin.

```sh
ke final/gds/counter_top.gds
```

![`counter_top` layout in KLayout (200 µm × 100 µm).](fig/counter_top/counter_top_black.png){#fig-counter-top-layout}

The LibreLane render is copied to [`render/img/counter_top_librelane.png`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/render/img/), and the high-resolution renders from `sak-render.py` are saved as `counter_top_white.png` and `counter_top_black.png` in the same folder. The verification reports are written to [`verification/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/verification/).

## RTL Mixed-Signal Simulation with Xschem

For an introduction to Ngspice and Verilog RTL co-simulation with Xschem, see Stefan Schippers' video: [Ngspice + Verilog Co-Simulation in Xschem](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PPd7jkcHOgA). This RTL mixed-signal simulation is currently not included in this repository, but it will be added in a future update.

## Gate-Level Mixed-Signal Simulation with Xschem

A more accurate validation step is the gate-level mixed-signal simulation in Xschem with the Ngspice XSPICE event-driven engine. The LibreLane-extracted SPICE netlist (`netlist/spice/<CELL>.spice`, copied from the latest run by `copy-netlist`) is converted into an XSPICE model with the following command, which is also executed automatically as part of `make build-top`.

```sh
make generate-xspice
```

The conversion pipeline is `.spice → .xspice` (`spi2xspice.py`), followed by a pin-reorder pass with `sak-pin-reorder.py` (a SAK tool installed in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container) to match the Xschem symbol
([`schematic/xschem/counter_top.sym`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/schematic/xschem/)).

::: {.callout-note}
The pins are matched **by name**: every pin in the Xschem symbol carries a `sim_pinname=<netlist_name>` property, so the alphabetically sorted ports of the extracted netlist are mapped correctly regardless of their order. Since `make build-top` regenerates the XSPICE model right after copying the netlists, the model always matches the current LibreLane run.
:::

### The symbol is a source file

The macro is hardened, so it has no schematic, and Xschem's "make symbol from a schematic" (key `a`) has nothing to work from. `schematic/xschem/counter_top.sym` is drawn by hand, and everything downstream bends to it: the pin order of the XSPICE model and of the extracted PEX netlists is sorted to match it. It is therefore never regenerated by a build. The testbench wires to pin **coordinates**, and a pin one grid step off its wire floats without any error, so a build that moved pins would quietly break the simulation instead of failing it.

Two targets support that arrangement without taking ownership of the file away from you.

```sh
make symbol-gl      # scaffold schematic/xschem/<CELL>.sym, for a new macro
make symbol-check   # verify the committed symbol, runs inside generate-xspice
```

`symbol-gl` reads the ports of the powered netlist `netlist/pnl/<CELL>.pnl.v` and writes a first-cut symbol in which every port is a pin with its direction, its bus range and its `sim_pinname`. The geometry follows Xschem's own symbol generator, so loading the result and saving it again returns it unchanged. It is a scaffold: rename the pins to house style (`clock_i` becomes `di_clock`, `counter_value_o[0..7]` becomes `do_b[0..7]`), arrange them, draw the body, then commit it. Renaming is safe because `sim_pinname` holds the binding to the netlist. The target refuses to overwrite an existing symbol, because that is where the hand work lives.

`symbol-check` is the half that runs in the build. It compares the committed symbol against the same netlist and fails if a port was added, removed, renamed, given a different width, or drawn with the wrong direction. Its most useful check is that **every pin declares `sim_pinname`**: a single pin missing the property drops `sak-pin-reorder.py` out of name matching and into matching by position, which is wrong for an alphabetically sorted netlist and can mis-wire the macro without any error at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
For a new digital macro the order is: harden it once, `make copy-netlist`, `make symbol-gl`, arrange the symbol in Xschem, and only then wire the testbench to it and run `make all`.
:::

### Running the gate-level testbench

The Xschem testbench ([`counter_top_tb_tran.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/testbenches/xschem/)) can be opened and simulated interactively.

```sh
cd testbenches/xschem
xschem counter_top_tb_tran.sch
```

![Xschem mixed-signal gate-level testbench `counter_top_tb_tran`.](fig/counter_top/counter_top_tb_tran_schematic.svg){#fig-counter-top-tb-tran-schematic}

In Xschem, hold **`Ctrl`** and click the **Simulate** button in the schematic to launch the simulator. Once the simulation has finished, you can hold **`Ctrl`** and click the **Load waves** arrow to load the simulation results into the integrated waveform viewer.

::: {.callout-tip}
This testbench also shows multiple ways to connect and display bus signals in Xschem. For more information, refer to the [Xschem documentation: Use Bus/Vector notation for signal bundles / arrays of instances](https://xschem.sourceforge.io/stefan/xschem_man/tutorial_busses.html).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
The green arrows in Xschem are called "launchers" and are essentially a series of Tcl commands. Since Xschem is fully scriptable via Tcl, repetitive tasks can be easily automated. Select a launcher and press `q` (Properties) to inspect or modify its underlying Tcl commands. This is also the beauty of Xschem and the reason why it is possible to also run simulations non-interactively, generate netlists, and run LVS with only Makefile targets, as you will see below.
:::

The same simulation can also be run non-interactively from the Makefile, and the result can be plotted from Python.

```sh
make sim-gl-xschem
make sim-view-xschem SCRIPT=plot_counter_top
```

`sim-gl-xschem` runs in batch mode: it netlists the testbench with `xschem netlist` and then calls `ngspice -b` directly, so `make` blocks until the run finishes and sees its exit status. The testbench is selected with `TB=<testbench_name>` (default: `<CELL>_tb_tran`). Since the run is headless, the `plot` commands in the testbench's `.control` block are a no-op. The testbench exports its results with `wrdata` to [`testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data), from where `sim-view-xschem` plots them with Matplotlib.

![Plotted Xschem simulation results of `counter_top_tb_tran` from `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/plot_counter_top.py`.](fig/counter_top/counter_top_tb_tran_sim.svg){#fig-counter-top-tb-tran-sim}

## Parasitic Extraction (PEX)

The XSPICE model above is a *gate-level* view of the macro: every standard cell becomes an XSPICE primitive driven by its Liberty delay, and the wiring is ideal. Parasitic extraction gives the *transistor-level* view instead. It reads the hardened layout [`final/gds/counter_top.gds`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/final/gds/) and writes a SPICE netlist into [`netlist/pex/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/counter/netlist/pex/) in which every standard cell is flattened to transistors and the wiring carries the resistances and capacitances measured from the layout.

```sh
make magic-pex                            # full-RC, the default EXT_MODE=3
make magic-pex EXT_MODE=1                 # C-decoupled, fastest
make klayout-pex                          # the same with kpex, which runs Magic internally
make magic-pex EXT_MODE=3 THRESHOLD=5000 MINRES=500 MINDELAY=2   # full-RC with custom extresist settings
```

Both targets read `final/gds/<CELL>.gds`, so `make build-top` (or at least `make copy-final`) has to have run first, and both abort with a clear message if it is missing. They start by running `make symbol-pex`, which derives `schematic/xschem/counter_top_pex.sym` from `counter_top.sym` so the PEX symbol can never go stale, and they finish by reordering the extracted `.subckt` ports to that symbol's pin order with `sak-pin-reorder.py` and verifying them with `scripts/check_pex_ports.py`. For `counter_top`, the full-RC default extracts 4401 transistors and roughly 2100 capacitors and 4600 resistors. Magic's `extresist` step is not deterministic, so the exact R and C counts move slightly from run to run while the transistor count stays the same.

The transient testbench already `.include`s the extracted netlist next to the XSPICE model, and it carries two spare DUT instances above the schematic, `x2` of `counter_top.sym` and `x3` of `counter_top_pex.sym`, both parked with `spice_ignore=true`. Swapping the wired-up `x1` for `x3` turns the run into a post-layout simulation.

::: {.callout-warning}
A post-layout run simulates every transistor of the macro. In the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container, 60 ns of transient take about 80 s, while the full 10 µs gate-level XSPICE run of the same testbench finishes in under 2 s. The XSPICE model stays the right tool for functional runs. Use the extracted netlist on short, targeted stimuli to check timing and signal integrity.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
The testbench uses looser Ngspice tolerances than the analog macro (`reltol=1e-3 abstol=1e-12 gmin=1e-12 rshunt=1e14`). Full-RC extraction splits the nets into fragments, and some of the resulting nodes have no DC path to ground, so with the analog macro's settings the post-layout run aborts at the initial timepoint with `Timestep too small`. The gate-level XSPICE run gives the same result either way.
:::

## Logic Equivalence Check {#sec-lec}

A gate-level simulation checks the netlist only for the stimuli of its testbench. A logic equivalence check (LEC) needs no testbench: a formal solver proves that the netlist does what the RTL does, for every input sequence. It catches a netlist that no longer matches the RTL, for example because the RTL was edited after the last `make build-top`, and any change of function by the flow.

```sh
make lec                         # final/nl/counter_top.nl.v against the RTL
make lec LEC_NETLIST=<netlist>   # another netlist, e.g. the synthesis netlist of a run
make lec LEC_TIMEOUT=<seconds>   # another time limit per partition (default: 300)
make lec-mutant                  # check that lec catches a difference
```

`make lec` writes an [EQY](https://github.com/YosysHQ/eqy) script to `flow/eqy/counter_top.eqy` and runs it in `flow/eqy/work/`. EQY pairs the signals of both designs by name, splits the design into partitions, and proves each of them. On the counter, these are 8 partitions, one per bit of `counter_value_o`, and the target exits with 0 only when all of them are equivalent. The RTL is read with a different front end than synthesis used, so that a front end that misreads the RTL cannot make the same mistake on both sides. The standard cells get their function from the Liberty file of the PDK, and a cell without a function fails the run.

`make lec-mutant` changes two copies of the netlist, one with a `sg13g2_nand2_1` swapped for a `sg13g2_nor2_1` and one with a flop clocked by `enable_i`. It passes only if a partition of `lec` reports `FAIL` on each: a check that cannot fail proves nothing, and neither does a `lec` that never ran a proof.

::: {.callout-tip}
## See it fail

Change `COUNTER_MAX_DEFAULT` in `rtl/constants.sv` from 255 to 199 and run `make lec` without rebuilding. The netlist is now stale, and EQY reports bits 3, 6 and 7 of `counter_value_o` as not equivalent. The counterexample is the waveform `trace.vcd` in `flow/eqy/work/strategies/<partition>/sby/<partition>/engine_0/`. It holds the counter at 199 with `enable_i` high: the RTL wraps to 0 and the netlist steps to 200, and these are the three bits that differ. Change the constant back afterwards.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
`make lec` has limits. It checks function, not timing, so static timing analysis and gate-level simulation stay. A register the RTL leaves unknown (`X`), for example after deleting its reset, matches any netlist. And because it pairs registers by name, it can fail on a correct netlist or run into its time limit: `sg13g2_dfrbpq_1` only resets to 0, so synthesis stores a register that resets to 1 inverted, and the match by name then compares the complement. Such a macro needs extra match rules.
:::

## Lint, Build, Verify and Simulate Everything

The full lint, build, verification, and simulation chain is run with the following command.

```sh
make all
```

This calls `lint-verilog-all`, `build-fpga`, `build-top`, `lec`, `lec-mutant`, `magic-pex`, and `sim-all` in sequence. The simulations run after the build, so the gate-level simulations run on the netlists, the XSPICE model and the extracted netlist produced by this build. `klayout-pex` is commented out in the recipe, since it is a second full extraction that nothing in the flow consumes. DRC and LVS are already covered by the LibreLane verification steps, so `lec` and `lec-mutant` are the only extra verification targets of the digital macro.

# Analog Macro Implementation {#sec-analog}

The [`inverter`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/) macro is the analog reference macro of the template. It is a 4-channel CMOS inverter, drawn at transistor level, and verified with a comprehensive verification chain:

- Layout vs. Schematic ([LVS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layout_versus_schematic)) with KLayout or Magic + Netgen,
- Design Rule Checking ([DRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_rule_checking)) with KLayout or Magic,
- Parasitic Extraction ([PEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasitic_extraction)) with KLayout or Magic,
- [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) simulation of process and mismatch variations with CACE.

Two instances are used in the chip core. One is used as a 4-channel digital inverter (`inverter1`), and the other as a 2-channel analog inverter (`inverter2`). See the [chip specifications](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/specifications.md) for the full picture.

::: {.callout-note}
An inverter can act as a digital circuit (when the input is driven by a digital signal and the output is switching between the supply rails). Here, we characterise the inverter as an analog circuit, meaning that we are interested in its continuous voltage transfer characteristic and its small-signal voltage gain.
:::

@fig-inverter-circuit shows the circuit of one channel. The NMOS $M_1$ and the PMOS $M_2$ form the complementary inverter. The transistors $M_\mathrm{dummy1}$ and $M_\mathrm{dummy2}$ are dummy devices. They do not contribute to the circuit function but improve matching in the layout, because the active transistors then see identical neighbouring structures on both sides.

![The CMOS inverter circuit with dummy transistors.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_circuit.svg){#fig-inverter-circuit width=45%}

## Getting Started with Xschem {#sec-xschem-intro}

Xschem is a schematic capture tool where circuits are built from symbols, wires, and net labels. Everything is stored in plain text files (`.sch` for schematics, `.sym` for symbols), which makes them friendly for version control and search-and-replace in a text editor.

Always start Xschem from the schematic or testbench folder of the macro, so that the local `xschemrc` is picked up. It sources the PDK configuration, adds the macro's schematic and testbench folders to the symbol search path, and pins the netlist directory to `testbenches/xschem/simulations/`, where Ngspice runs and writes its results.

```sh
cd macros/inverter/schematic/xschem
xschem                  # empty session
xschem inverter.sch     # or load a schematic directly at startup
```

The most important shortcuts are listed in @tbl-xschem-keys. A complete list is available in Xschem under `Help > Keys` and in the [Xschem Cheatsheet](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#sec-xschem-cheatsheet).

| Shortcut | Action |
| :--- | :--- |
| `Ins` | Insert a symbol from the component library |
| `w` | Draw a wire |
| `m` | Move the selected objects |
| `c` | Copy the selected objects |
| `Del` | Delete the selected objects |
| `q` | Edit the properties of the selected object |
| `Shift + R` | Rotate the selection |
| `Shift + F` / `Shift + V` | Mirror the selection horizontally / vertically |
| `u` / `Shift + U` | Undo / redo |
| `f` | Zoom full |
| `Ctrl + s` | Save |
| `Ctrl + o` | Open a schematic or symbol |
| `e` | Descend into the schematic of the selected symbol |
| `i` | Descend into the symbol view of the selected symbol |
| `Ctrl + e` | Return to the parent schematic |
| `a` | Make a symbol from the current schematic |
| `Shift + T` | Toggle the `spice_ignore` flag on the selected instances (excluded from the netlist) |
| `n` | Generate a netlist |

: Essential Xschem shortcuts. {#tbl-xschem-keys}

::: {.callout-tip}
Since Xschem is a text-based schematic editor, you can also open `*.sch` and `*.sym` files in a text editor and modify them there. This is especially useful for search-and-replace operations.
:::

## Schematic-Level Simulation

Go to the Xschem testbench folder and start Xschem.

```sh
cd macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem
xschem
xschem <testbench_name>.sch # load a testbench schematic directly at startup
```

Four testbenches are available in
[`testbenches/xschem/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/).

- [`inverter_tb_tran.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_tb_tran.sch), single-channel transient response (see @fig-inverter-tb-tran-schematic),
- [`inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch), open-loop ac characterisation (see @fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-schematic),
- [`inverter_tb_dc_vout.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_tb_dc_vout.sch), dc input sweep (see @fig-inverter-tb-dc-vout-schematic),
- [`inverter_top_tb_tran.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_top_tb_tran.sch), top-level transient on `inverter_top` (see @fig-inverter-top-tb-tran-schematic).

Load a testbench in Xschem by pressing **`Ctrl + o`**. Each testbench is operated with the three launcher buttons in the schematic. Hold **`Ctrl`** and click **Simulate** to netlist the schematic and start Ngspice. Once the simulation has finished, hold **`Ctrl`** and click **Load waves** to load the results into the integrated waveform viewer (the embedded graphs), or **Annotate OP** to back-annotate the operating point into the schematic. **Simulate** also regenerates the FET `.save` file described in @sec-tb-ac, so the operating-point annotation always matches the devices currently in the schematic. The following figures show the testbench schematics, the plotted results follow in @sec-batch-sim.

![Xschem testbench `inverter_tb_tran` (single-channel transient response on `inverter`).](fig/inverter_top/inverter_tb_tran_schematic.svg){#fig-inverter-tb-tran-schematic}

![Xschem testbench `inverter_tb_ac_ol` (open-loop ac characterisation on `inverter`).](fig/inverter_top/inverter_tb_ac_ol_schematic.svg){#fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-schematic}

![Xschem testbench `inverter_tb_dc_vout` (dc input sweep on `inverter`).](fig/inverter_top/inverter_tb_dc_vout_schematic.svg){#fig-inverter-tb-dc-vout-schematic}

![Xschem top-level testbench `inverter_top_tb_tran` (transient on `inverter_top`).](fig/inverter_top/inverter_top_tb_tran_schematic.svg){#fig-inverter-top-tb-tran-schematic}

### Anatomy of the AC Testbench {#sec-tb-ac}

We look at the ac testbench in detail, because it contains every ingredient a complete analog testbench needs. Open [`inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch) (see @fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-schematic) and identify the following parts:

**1. The device under test.** An instance `x1` of `inverter.sym`. Two spare instances `x2` (`inverter.sym`) and `x3` (`inverter_pex.sym`) are also placed, with the attribute `spice_ignore=true` so they are excluded from the netlist. They are used later for the post-layout comparison in @sec-postlayout.

**2. Supplies and bias.** A voltage source `VDD` with `value={VDD}` powers the circuit between the `VDD` rail and ground. The input source `vin` has the value

```spice
dc {Vcm} ac 1
```

The `dc {Vcm}` part biases the input at the switching threshold $V_\mathrm{cm} = V_\mathrm{DD}/2$, where the inverter has its highest gain. The `ac 1` part sets the small-signal stimulus amplitude to $1\,\mathrm{V}$. This does not overdrive the circuit, because the ac analysis linearises the circuit around the operating point. With an input of exactly 1, the output magnitude directly equals the voltage gain, so `v(vout)/v(vin)` is a normalised transfer function.

**3. The load.** A capacitor `C1` with `value={Cload}` ($10\,\mathrm{pF}$) loads the output. A load resistor `R1` with `value={Rload}` is placed as well but disabled with `spice_ignore=true`. Toggle it with `Shift + T` if you want to study resistive loading.

**4. The model includes.** A `code_shown.sym` block named `MODEL` pulls in the PDK device models with the typical corner:

```spice
.lib cornerMOSlv.lib mos_tt
.lib cornerMOShv.lib mos_tt
.lib cornerHBT.lib hbt_typ
.lib cornerRES.lib res_typ
.lib cornerCAP.lib cap_typ
.lib cornerDIO.lib dio_tt
```

The bare file names work because the container points Ngspice at the `.spiceinit` of the active PDK (`$PDK_ROOT/$PDK/libs.tech/ngspice/.spiceinit`), which adds the PDK model directory to the Ngspice source path and loads the compiled PSP OSDI models. To simulate a different process corner, replace `mos_tt` with, for example, `mos_ss` or `mos_ff`.

**5. The control block.** A second `code_shown.sym` block named `NGSPICE` contains the parameters, simulator options, and the `.control` section:

```spice
.include ../../../netlist/pex/inverter_magic_pex_3.spice
.param VDD=1.5
.param Vcm=VDD/2
.temp 27
.param Cload=10p
.param Rload=1k
.options savecurrents klu method=gear reltol=1e-4 abstol=1e-15 gmin=1e-15
.control
save all

* User Constants
let f_min = 0.1
let f_max = 10G
let fdc = 1

* Operating Point Analysis
op
remzerovec
write @schname.raw
set appendwrite

* AC Analysis
ac dec 101 $&const.f_min $&const.f_max
remzerovec
write @schname.raw
...
.endc
```

Read it top to bottom:

- The `.include` line loads the extracted PEX netlist from [`netlist/pex/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/netlist/pex/), which defines the subcircuit `inverter_pex`. It is not used while `x1` is active, but it must be present for the post-layout swap in @sec-postlayout. The extracted netlists are tracked in the repository, so a fresh clone simulates right away, and `make magic-pex CELL=inverter` refreshes them (see @sec-pex).
- The `.param` lines define the supply, the input bias, and the load as parameters, so one edit changes the whole testbench. The `.temp` line sets the simulation temperature in °C. It is an Ngspice directive of its own, not a parameter.
- The `.options` line selects the KLU sparse solver and tightens the tolerances for a clean ac result.
- Inside `.control`, first an operating point analysis (`op`) runs and its result is written to the `.raw` file. This is what **Annotate OP** reads.
- Then the ac analysis sweeps 101 points per decade from $0.1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $10\,\mathrm{GHz}$ and appends the result to the same `.raw` file.

**6. The measurements.** After the analysis, the control block computes the open-loop gain and extracts the key numbers:

```spice
let Aol = v(vout)/v(vin)
let Aol_dB = vdb(Aol)
let Aol_arg = 180/PI*cphase(Aol)

* DC open-loop gain
meas ac Adc_ol_dB find Aol_dB when frequency = fdc

* 3dB cut-off frequency
let Aol_fc = Adc_ol_dB - 3
meas ac fc find frequency when Aol_dB = Aol_fc

* Unity Gain Bandwidth (Aol=1 or Aol_dB = 0dB)
meas ac UGB when Aol_dB=0 fall=1

* Phase Margin at Aol=1 or Aol_dB = 0dB
meas ac arg_0dB find Aol_arg when Aol_dB=0
let PM = 180-abs(arg_0dB)
```

The phase starts at $180°$ because the inverter is an inverting amplifier. With the sizing from @sec-sizing you should measure approximately $A_\mathrm{ol} = 31.3\,\mathrm{dB}$, $f_\mathrm{c} = 2.9\,\mathrm{MHz}$, and $\mathrm{UGB} = 107\,\mathrm{MHz}$ (see @fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-sim).

**7. The data export.** The final `wrdata` command writes the traces to [`plot_simulations/data/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data), so the Python plotting script and the batch flow from @sec-batch-sim can use them.

**8. Graphs and the save file.** The embedded graph boxes display magnitude and phase after **Load waves**. A small `SAVE` code block pulls in the FET save file:

```spice
.include [file rootname [file tail [xschem get schname]]].save
```

The Tcl expression evaluates to the bare file name of the current schematic, for example `inverter_tb_ac_ol.save`, so the include resolves inside `testbenches/xschem/simulations/`, where Ngspice runs. That file holds a `.save` line for every transistor parameter (`ids`, `gm`, `gds`, `vth`, ...), which is what the `annotate_fet_params` symbols inside the inverter and the **Annotate OP** launcher read back from the `.raw` file. Without it, Ngspice would not store these internal device quantities and the annotation would stay empty.

You never have to create the file by hand: both the **Simulate** launcher and `make sim-xschem` (see @sec-batch-sim) write it before every run with `write_data [save_params]`. Since `testbenches/xschem/simulations/` is generated and git-ignored, a fresh clone works right away. Xschem's **IHP > Create FET .save file** menu entry writes the same file manually.

::: {.callout-tip}
The dc and transient testbenches follow exactly the same pattern. Only the analysis command changes: `dc Vgsp 0 $&VDD 1m` sweeps the input source in $1\,\mathrm{mV}$ steps, and `tran 1u 5m` simulates $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ with a sine input `sin({Vcm} 10m 1k)`, a $10\,\mathrm{mV}$ amplitude at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Both testbenches add a `.csparam VDD=VDD` line next to the `.param` line, because a parameter is visible inside the `.control` block (as `$&VDD`) only through `.csparam`. In the dc sweep, at which input voltage does `vout` cross $V_\mathrm{cm} = 0.75\,\mathrm{V}$? The simulation reports approximately $0.745\,\mathrm{V}$, slightly below $V_\mathrm{DD}/2$.
:::

### Batch Simulation with the Makefile {#sec-batch-sim}

Every testbench can also be run non-interactively through the Makefile, which is useful for reproducible results and scripting.

```sh
cd macros/inverter
make sim-xschem                         # run the default testbench (inverter_top_tb_tran)
make sim-xschem TB=<testbench_name>     # run another testbench non-interactively
make sim-view-xschem SCRIPT=plot_inverter      # plot results of inverter with Python
make sim-view-xschem SCRIPT=plot_inverter_top  # plot results of inverter_top with Python
```

`sim-xschem` runs in batch mode: it netlists the testbench with `xschem netlist` and then calls `ngspice -b` directly, so `make` blocks until the run finishes and sees its exit status. The testbench is selected with `TB=<testbench_name>` and defaults to `<CELL>_tb_tran`. Since the run is headless, the `plot` commands in the testbench's `.control` block are a no-op. Every testbench exports its results with `wrdata` to [`testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data) instead.

The Makefile target `sim-view-xschem` calls the Python plotters in [`testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations), selected with the `SCRIPT` variable (default: `plot_<CELL>`), to parse the raw simulation output and plot the results with Matplotlib. The following figures show some of these plotted results.

![Plotted simulation result of `inverter_tb_ac_ol`.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_tb_ac_ol_sim.svg){#fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-sim width=90%}

![Plotted simulation result of `inverter_tb_dc_vout`.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_tb_dc_vout_sim.svg){#fig-inverter-tb-dc-vout-sim width=80%}

![Plotted simulation result of `inverter_top_tb_tran`.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_top_tb_tran_sim.svg){#fig-inverter-top-tb-tran-sim width=80%}

::: {.callout-tip}
The full simulation suite, including all four testbenches plus the CACE flow (see @sec-cace), is triggered with `make sim-all`.
:::

## Schematic-Level Drawing

To inspect or modify the underlying circuit of a symbol, mark the symbol and press **`e`** to descend into the underlying circuit, then **`Ctrl + e`** to go back up. To inspect or modify the graphical symbol of a device, mark the symbol and press **`i`** to descend into the symbol drawing, then **`Ctrl + e`** to go back up again.

### Drawing the Inverter Schematic {#sec-draw-schematic}

@fig-inverter-schematic displays the schematic of the `inverter` cell with additional small-signal parameters for the NMOS and PMOS transistors at the chosen operating point. To view these small-signal parameters, hold **`Ctrl`** and click **Annotate OP** after the simulation has finished. Afterwards, descend into the inverter schematic.

![Xschem `inverter` schematic with dummy transistors and OP annotations.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_schematic.svg){#fig-inverter-schematic width=65%}

To draw this schematic from scratch, start Xschem in `macros/inverter/schematic/xschem/` and go through the following steps. The reference is [`inverter.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/schematic/xschem/inverter.sch), and the device geometry comes from the sizing in @sec-sizing (see @tbl-inverter-sizing-geom).

1. **Place the transistors.** Press `Ins`, and pick `sg13_lv_nmos.sym` and `sg13_lv_pmos.sym` from the `sg13g2_pr` PDK library. Place the NMOS $M_1$ at the bottom and the PMOS $M_2$ at the top.
2. **Set the device parameters.** Select a transistor and press `q`. Enter the values from @tbl-inverter-sizing-geom, for example for $M_1$: `l=1.0u`, `w=20.0u`, `ng=20`, `m=1`. Note that `w` is the total width and `ng` is the number of fingers. Keep `spiceprefix=X`, because the PSP transistor models of the PDK are SPICE subcircuits and must be instantiated with an `X` prefix. Keep `mm_ok=1` as well, it is the per-instance switch of the PDK's mismatch models, which the CACE mismatch runs in @sec-cace rely on.
3. **Place the dummy transistors.** Copy each device with `c` and change the properties to the dummy sizing (`w=2.0u`, `ng=2` for the NMOS and `w=12.0u`, `ng=2` for the PMOS). Wire all four terminals of each dummy to its supply rail (gate, source, drain, and bulk of $M_\mathrm{dummy1}$ to `VSS`, those of $M_\mathrm{dummy2}$ to `VDD`), so the dummies are off and only their geometry matters.
4. **Wire the circuit.** Press `w` and connect the gates of $M_1$ and $M_2$ to the input net, the drains to the output net, the NMOS source and bulk to `VSS`, and the PMOS source and bulk to `VDD`.
5. **Add the pins.** Press `Ins` and place `ipin.sym` for the input `vin`, `iopin.sym` for the output `vout`, and `iopin.sym` for `VDD` and `VSS`. The pin names define the port names of the subcircuit later used for LVS, so name them exactly `vin`, `vout`, `VDD`, and `VSS`.
6. **Annotate (optional).** Place `annotate_fet_params.sym` next to $M_1$ and $M_2$ and set `ref=M1` and `ref=M2`. After a simulation, these display the operating-point parameters of the devices directly in the schematic, as visible in @fig-inverter-schematic.
7. **Save** with `Ctrl + s` as `inverter.sch`.

### Drawing the Inverter Symbol {#sec-draw-symbol}

To use the inverter in a testbench or in the 4-channel `inverter_top.sch`, it needs a symbol. @fig-inverter-symbol shows the finished symbol, the reference is [`inverter.sym`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/schematic/xschem/inverter.sym).

![Xschem `inverter` symbol.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_symbol.svg){#fig-inverter-symbol width=30%}

1. **Auto-generate the symbol.** With `inverter.sch` open, press `a`. Xschem creates `inverter.sym` with one pin per schematic pin, placed on a rectangular outline.
2. **Open the symbol.** Load it with `Ctrl + o` (or select a placed instance and press `i`).
3. **Redraw the shape.** Delete the auto-generated rectangle and draw the triangle with the output bubble using the line (`l`) and arc tools. Keep the pin boxes, they carry the electrical information (`name` and `dir` attributes).
4. **Arrange the pins.** Place `vin` on the left, `vout` on the right, `VDD` on top, and `VSS` at the bottom. Add the small text labels with `t`.
5. **Check the global properties.** Press `q` with nothing selected. The symbol must have `type=subcircuit` and `format="@name @pinlist @symname"`. With `type=subcircuit`, Xschem descends into `inverter.sch` during netlisting and emits the full transistor-level subcircuit. Keep the `spectre_format` line that Xschem wrote next to it, see the note in @sec-pex.
6. **Save** the symbol.

You can now place the symbol in any schematic with `Ins`. The 4-channel [`inverter_top.sch`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/schematic/xschem/inverter_top.sch) places four instances of it, and its symbol `inverter_top.sym` is drawn the same way. The PEX symbols `inverter_pex.sym` and `inverter_top_pex.sym` are not drawn by hand, `make symbol-pex` derives them (see @sec-pex).

## Process Variation and Mismatch (CACE) {#sec-cace}

[CACE](https://github.com/fossi-foundation/cace) drives Ngspice via a
characterisation YAML file ([`verification/cace/inverter.yaml`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/verification/cace/inverter.yaml)) to run Monte Carlo simulations and produce process and mismatch variation plots.

```sh
make sim-cace
```

Plots are written to [`verification/cace/results/inverter/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/verification/cace/results/inverter).
This step is mainly relevant for advanced designers who want to characterise the analog macro across PVT corners. The following figures show the results of the CACE simulations for 200 iterations.

@fig-inverter-cace-aol shows the process (left) and mismatch (right) variations of the dc open-loop gain $A_\mathrm{ol}$, while @fig-inverter-cace-aol-vdd plots its variation across several process corners at one fixed supply voltage.

::: {#fig-inverter-cace-aol layout-ncol=2 fig-cap="CACE process (left) and mismatch (right) variations of $A_\\mathrm{ol}$."}
![Process variation of $A_\mathrm{ol}$.](fig/inverter_top/Adc_ol_dB_mc.png){width=100%}

![Mismatch variation of $A_\mathrm{ol}$.](fig/inverter_top/Adc_ol_dB_mm.png){width=100%}
:::

![CACE variation of $A_\mathrm{ol}$ across several process corners.](fig/inverter_top/Adc_ol_dB_vs_vdd.png){#fig-inverter-cace-aol-vdd width=75%}

@fig-inverter-cace-fcu shows the process (left) and mismatch (right) variations of the open-loop lower cut-off frequency $f_\mathrm{cu}$, while @fig-inverter-cace-fcu-vdd plots its variation across several process corners at one fixed supply voltage.

::: {#fig-inverter-cace-fcu layout-ncol=2 fig-cap="CACE process (left) and mismatch (right) variations of $f_\\mathrm{cu}$."}
![Process variation of $f_\mathrm{cu}$.](fig/inverter_top/fcu_mc.png){width=100%}

![Mismatch variation of $f_\mathrm{cu}$.](fig/inverter_top/fcu_mm.png){width=100%}
:::

![CACE variation of $f_\mathrm{cu}$ across several process corners.](fig/inverter_top/fcu_vs_vdd.png){#fig-inverter-cace-fcu-vdd width=75%}

::: {.callout-note}
Note that the above process and mismatch variation results are poor for an analog circuit. Also, the open-loop gain varies significantly across corners. This is because the example is only a simple inverter without a compensation technique. For a practical single-ended inverter amplifier, one would at least add a feedback resistor from output to input to stabilise the operating point and therefore the gain across corners. If you want to see improved variation results, you can try adding a feedback resistor in the `inverter.sch` schematic and running the CACE flow again.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
In the `inverter.yaml` characterisation file, more parameter sweeps can be added, for example, across temperature, supply voltages or load capacitance.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Do not `print()` from a CACE postprocess hook. The hooks in [`verification/cace/scripts/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/verification/cace/scripts/) post-process the raw Ngspice results before CACE evaluates them against the specification, and CACE 2.11.0 redirects their stdout into its own rich logger, which writes back to stdout. The first `print()` therefore recurses without end, and `make sim-cace` hangs instead of failing. That is why the debug prints in [`inverter_tb_ac.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/verification/cace/scripts/inverter_tb_ac.py) are commented out. Write intermediate values to a file if you need to inspect them.
:::

## Transistor Sizing {#sec-sizing}

During simulation, it could happen that some specifications are not fulfilled and that the inverter must be resized. In this tutorial, the inverter is sized with the $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ method (see [Transistor Sizing Using $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ Methodology](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#sec-gmid-method) for theoretical background).
