Instead of relying on textbook square-law equations, the method looks up the actual device behaviour from pre-characterised SPICE simulations, parameterised by $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$. An overview of these techsweeps can be found in the folder [`doc/sizing/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/doc/sizing). The chosen $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ point sets the inversion level of the transistor and therefore the trade-off between intrinsic gain (high $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$, weak inversion) and bandwidth (low $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$, strong inversion). These trade-offs are discussed in @sec-tradeoffs. For each chosen operating point the lookup tables return all relevant figures of merit ($I_\mathrm{D}/W$, $g_\mathrm{m}/g_\mathrm{ds}$, $g_\mathrm{m}/C_\mathrm{gg}$, $S_\mathrm{TH}$, etc.) at the actual bias condition, which is then used to compute $W$ for a given drain current.

### Design Trade-offs: Choosing $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ and $L$ {#sec-tradeoffs}

Before sizing anything, two numbers have to be picked: the transconductance efficiency $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ and the channel length $L$. Everything else follows from them, so it is worth understanding what each one buys and what it costs.

$g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ says how much transconductance you get per ampere of bias current, in $\mathrm{S/A}$ or $\mathrm{V^{-1}}$. It is a normalised, technology-independent measure of the **inversion level** of the device.

@fig-tradeoffs shows the trade-offs in one picture. The arrows point from the centre towards the corner where each design parameter reaches its **best** value, so the same parameter is at its worst in the opposite direction.

![Overview of key design trade-offs depending on the channel length $L$ and the transconductance efficiency $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$. Taken from [Tradeoffs in Saturation](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#sec-tradeoffs-saturation) in the Analog Circuit Design course at JKU.](fig/inverter_top/tradeoffs_gmid.svg){#fig-tradeoffs width=75%}

Read it corner by corner:

- **Strong inversion, short $L$** (bottom left): $f_\mathrm{T}$ and input impedance $Z_\mathrm{in}$ are maximal, gate capacitance $C_\mathrm{gg}$ and area are minimal. This is the high-speed corner.
- **Strong inversion, medium $L$** (left): minimal thermal noise PSD $S_\mathrm{TH}$ and maximal current density $I_\mathrm{D}/W$.
- **Moderate inversion, short $L$** (bottom): the speed-efficiency product $f_\mathrm{T} \cdot g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ is maximal, the best overall compromise between bandwidth and current.
- **Moderate inversion, long $L$** (top): the output resistance $r_\mathrm{ds} = 1/g_\mathrm{ds}$ is maximal. This is where current sources belong.
- **Weak inversion, long $L$** (top right): intrinsic gain $g_\mathrm{m}/g_\mathrm{ds}$ is maximal, while flicker corner frequency $f_\mathrm{co}$, noise factor $\gamma$, flicker noise $S_\mathrm{FL}$, offset $V_\mathrm{OS}$, and power $P$ are minimal. This is the low-power, low-noise, high-gain corner.
- **Weak inversion, medium $L$** (right): overdrive $V_\mathrm{od}$ and $V_\mathrm{ds,sat}$ are minimal, so this corner gives the most voltage headroom.

Two corners stay empty on purpose. Strong inversion with a long channel and weak inversion with a short channel optimise nothing, they combine the drawbacks of both settings, so in practice they make little sense.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rules of thumb

Fast circuits use **strong inversion with short channels**. Low-power and low-noise circuits use **weak inversion with long channels**. Current sources use **moderate inversion with longer channels**, to maximise their output resistance. Everything else starts in moderate inversion and is moved from there.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Where does our inverter sit?

The sizing below lands at $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D} = 3.76\,\mathrm{V^{-1}}$ with $L = 1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, which is deep strong inversion with a comparatively long channel, that is the corner the map leaves empty. This is a deliberate compromise for this example, not an oversight: the stage has to drive a $10\,\mathrm{pF}$ load, which demands a lot of $g_\mathrm{m}$ and therefore a lot of current, while the long channel keeps the intrinsic gain and the matching of this very simple circuit acceptable. It also explains the modest simulated gain of about $31\,\mathrm{dB}$. Keep the map in mind when you size your own blocks, where you are free to choose the operating point rather than inheriting it.
:::

### Sizing the Inverter {#sec-sizing-inverter}

The full sizing flow for the inverter is implemented in the Jupyter notebook [`scripts/sizing/sizing_inverter.ipynb`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/scripts/sizing/sizing_inverter.ipynb). The notebook uses [`pygmid`](https://github.com/dreoilin/pygmid) to query the pre-characterised ihp-sg13g2 NMOS/PMOS lookup tables ([`sg13g2_lv_nmos.mat`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/scripts/sizing/data/sg13g2_lv_nmos.mat) and [`sg13g2_lv_pmos.mat`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/scripts/sizing/data/sg13g2_lv_pmos.mat)). An overview of the $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ MOSFET characterisation procedure can be found [here](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html#sec-techsweep-testbench).

The Jupyter notebook `sizing_inverter.ipynb` runs through the following steps:

1. Define the design targets: $V_\mathrm{DD} = 1.5\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_\mathrm{cm,in} = V_\mathrm{cm,out} = V_\mathrm{DD}/2 = 0.75\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_\mathrm{out} = 0.75\,\mathrm{mA}$, $C_\mathrm{load} = 10\,\mathrm{pF}$ and $L = 1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. $L$ is chosen longer than the minimum to increase intrinsic gain and reduce mismatch, but at the cost of increased area and reduced bandwidth.
2. Look up $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$, $g_\mathrm{m}/g_\mathrm{ds}$, $g_\mathrm{m}/C_\mathrm{gg}$ and $I_\mathrm{D}/W$ based on $L$ and the operating-point voltages.
3. Compute the required widths $W = I_\mathrm{D} / (I_\mathrm{D}/W)$ for NMOS and PMOS, and derive the resulting $W_\mathrm{PMOS}/W_\mathrm{NMOS}$ ratio.
4. Round the continuous widths to a practical finger configuration with equal finger counts for NMOS and PMOS (for better layout matching) and recompute the small-signal parameters with the final widths.
5. Estimate the open-loop gain $A_\mathrm{ol} = -g_\mathrm{m,tot} / g_\mathrm{ds,tot}$ and the output resistance $R_\mathrm{out} = 1/g_\mathrm{ds,tot}$ of the complementary inverter stage.

The resulting device geometry is summarised in @tbl-inverter-sizing-geom.

| Device  | $L$ ($\mathrm{\mu m}$) | Fingers ($\mathrm{NF}$) | $W$ / Finger ($\mathrm{\mu m}$) | Total $W$ ($\mathrm{\mu m}$) |
| :------ | :----------------------: | :-----------------: | :-------------------------------: | :----------------------------: |
| NMOS $M_1$ | 1.0                   | 20              | 1.0                               | 20.0                           |
| PMOS $M_2$ | 1.0                   | 20              | 6.0                               | 120.0                          |
| NMOS $M_\mathrm{dummy1}$ | 1.0     | 2               | 1.0                               | 2.0                            |
| PMOS $M_\mathrm{dummy2}$ | 1.0     | 2               | 6.0                               | 12.0                           |

: Sized device geometry of the complementary inverter and its dummy devices. {#tbl-inverter-sizing-geom}

With these final widths the notebook computes the small-signal parameters listed in @tbl-inverter-sizing-ss. As a reference, compare these values with the OP annotations in @fig-inverter-schematic.

| Parameter                                                  | NMOS $M_1$      | PMOS $M_2$      | Inverter (NMOS $\parallel$ PMOS)        |
| :--------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------: | :-------------: | :-------------------------------------: |
| Drain current $I_\mathrm{D}$ ($\mathrm{mA}$)                                           | 0.89       | 0.78       | --                               |
| Transconductance efficiency $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ ($\mathrm{V^{-1}}$)            | 3.76       | 3.76       | --                               |
| Inversion level                                                                        | strong     | strong     | --                               |
| Transconductance $g_\mathrm{m}$ ($\mathrm{mS}$)                                        | 3.35       | 2.92       | --                               |
| Output conductance $g_\mathrm{ds}$ ($\mathrm{\mu S}$)                                | 116        | 29         | --                               |
| Gate capacitance $C_\mathrm{gg}$ ($\mathrm{fF}$)                                        | 154.32     | 824.86     | --                               |
| Transit frequency $f_\mathrm{T} = g_\mathrm{m}/(2\pi\,C_\mathrm{gg})$ ($\mathrm{GHz}$)  | 2.91       | 0.54       | --                               |
| Thermal noise PSD $S_\mathrm{TH}$ at $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ($\mathrm{pV^2/Hz}$)              | 38.95      | 73.98      | --                               |
| Flicker corner frequency $f_\mathrm{co}$ ($\mathrm{MHz}$)                               | 3.87       | 2.28       | --                               |
| $g_\mathrm{m,tot} = g_\mathrm{m,NMOS} + g_\mathrm{m,PMOS}$ ($\mathrm{mS}$)              | --         | --         | 6.28                             |
| $g_\mathrm{ds,tot} = g_\mathrm{ds,NMOS} + g_\mathrm{ds,PMOS}$ ($\mathrm{\mu S}$)      | --         | --         | 145                              |

: Calculated small-signal parameters with final widths. {#tbl-inverter-sizing-ss}

From these values, the open-loop dc gain $A_\mathrm{ol}$, the output resistance $R_\mathrm{out}$, the open-loop cut-off frequency $f_\mathrm{cu}$, and the unity-gain frequency $f_\mathrm{T}$ with a dominant capacitive load $C_\mathrm{load} = 10\,\mathrm{pF}$ can be estimated as

$$
|A_\mathrm{ol}| = \frac{g_\mathrm{m,tot}}{g_\mathrm{ds,tot}} = \frac{6.28\,\mathrm{mS}}{145\,\mathrm{\mu S}} = 43.2 = 32.72\,\mathrm{dB},
$$

$$
R_\mathrm{out} = \frac{1}{g_\mathrm{ds,tot}} = \frac{1}{145\,\mathrm{\mu S}} = 6.89\,\mathrm{k\Omega},
$$

$$
f_\mathrm{cu} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_\mathrm{out}\,C_\mathrm{load}} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 6.89\,\mathrm{k\Omega} \cdot 10\,\mathrm{pF}} = 2.31\,\mathrm{MHz},
$$

$$
f_\mathrm{T} = \frac{g_\mathrm{m,tot}}{2\pi\,C_\mathrm{load}} = \frac{6.28\,\mathrm{mS}}{2\pi \cdot 10\,\mathrm{pF}} = 100\,\mathrm{MHz}.
$$

@tbl-inverter-sizing-vs-ac compares these hand-calculated values against the open-loop ac simulation result from [`inverter_tb_ac_ol`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/testbenches/xschem/inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch) (see @fig-inverter-tb-ac-ol-sim).

| Quantity                  | $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ calculation | ac open-loop simulation |
| :------------------------ | :-------------------------------------: | :---------------------: |
| Open-loop dc gain $A_\mathrm{ol}$ | $32.72\,\mathrm{dB}$                | $31.33\,\mathrm{dB}$   |
| Open-loop cut-off frequency $f_\mathrm{cu}$   | $2.31\,\mathrm{MHz}$                | $2.89\,\mathrm{MHz}$   |
| Unity-gain frequency $f_\mathrm{T}$ | $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$            | $107\,\mathrm{MHz}$    |

: Calculated vs. simulated open-loop characteristics of the inverter. {#tbl-inverter-sizing-vs-ac}

::: {.callout-tip}
The notebook is fully parametric. Changing $L$, the target $g_\mathrm{m}/I_\mathrm{D}$ or $I_\mathrm{out}$ and re-running the cells immediately produces a new sizing point, so it can be used as a starting template for sizing other simple analog blocks with the ihp-sg13g2 lookup tables. Try it out yourself by decreasing the transistor length to $L = 0.5\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ and see how the small-signal parameters and the resulting open-loop gain and cut-off frequency change. What would you expect based on the trade-offs above?
:::

## Getting Started with KLayout {#sec-klayout-intro}

The layout is created and edited in KLayout. Open it in edit mode with `ke`, an alias for `klayout -e` provided by the container. With the ihp-sg13g2 PDK active, KLayout loads the `sg13g2` technology, which brings the layer properties, the `SG13_dev` PCell library, and the `SG13G2 PDK` menu with the DRC and LVS runners.

```sh
ke                              # empty session
ke layout/inverter_top.klay.gds # or open a layout directly at startup
```

Some basics before drawing:

- **Database unit.** When creating a new layout (`File > New Layout`), set the database unit (DBU) to $0.001\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. This is important for the IHP Open-PDK. The [KLayout cheatsheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/klayout/klayout_cheatsheet.md) explains how to rescale a layout that was started with the wrong DBU.
- **Layer roles.** Each drawing layer has three roles: `MetalX.drawing` carries the actual geometry, `MetalX.pin` marks the pin shapes, and `MetalX.text` carries the pin labels used by LVS.
- **PCells.** The PDK provides parametric cells (PCells) in the `SG13_dev` library, for example `nmos`, `pmos`, resistors (`rppd`, `rsil`, `rhigh`), capacitors (`cmim`, `moscap_n`, `moscap_p`), taps (`ntap1`, `ptap1`), the `guard_ring`, and `via_stack`. Select a placed PCell and press `Q` to edit its parameters.

The most important shortcuts are listed in @tbl-klayout-keys, taken from the [KLayout cheatsheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/klayout/klayout_cheatsheet.md) in this repository.

| Shortcut | Action |
| :--- | :--- |
| `Q` | Properties of the selected object / PCell |
| `M` | Move quickly |
| `A` | Align tool |
| `C` | Copy object |
| `P` | Path / drawing tool (double-click to finish) |
| `R` | Draw rectangle |
| `T` | Place text |
| `Shift + P` | Set pin (input, output, ...) for LVS |
| `O` | Place vias during routing (path mode) |
| `E` / `Ctrl + E` | Descend into / ascend from an instance |
| `Shift + R` | Rotate instance by 90° |
| `Shift + H` / `Shift + V` | Flip instance horizontally / vertically |
| `F` | Zoom full |
| `U` / `Shift + U` | Undo / redo |
| `K` / `Shift + K` | Ruler+ / clear all rulers |
| `0` ... `9` | Layer focus (see @tbl-klayout-plugins) |

: Essential KLayout shortcuts with the productivity plugins installed. {#tbl-klayout-keys}

Most of these shortcuts come from the [KLayout Productivity Suite](https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-productivity-suite), a collection of plugins developed at JKU that make manual layout much faster. The suite is installed in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container, so nothing has to be set up. The full documentation with animations is [here](https://iic-jku.github.io/klayout-productivity-suite/doc/doc.html). A short summary:

| Plugin | What it does |
| :----- | :----------- |
| **Move Quickly Tool** (`M`) | Rapid repositioning of shapes and instances with mouse or keyboard, including diagonal moves and multi-object selection |
| **Align Tool** (`A`) | Align objects to each other by clicking reference features (middle, corner, or edge markers) |
| **Pin Tool** (`Shift + P`) | Place LVS-ready pins (pin shape plus text label) with automatic layer detection from the current layer selection |
| **Layer Shortcuts** (`0` ... `9`) | Fast layer visibility switching: `1` ... `7` focus on one metal with its vias, `8` gate poly, `9` diffusion, `0` shows the default layers, `,` hides them, `Shift + 1` ... `Shift + 9` extend the current focus by one more layer group |
| **Netlist Import** (`File > Import > Netlist`) | Import a SPICE netlist and place the cell instances with technology-specific mapping. Great for starting a layout from the schematic netlist |
| **Library Manager** (`File > Cell Library Manager`) | Manage hierarchical layouts and cell libraries, and export a clean layout for tapeout |
| **Auto Backup** (`File > Automatic Backups`) | Periodic layout backups with configurable interval and rotation |
| **Vector File Export** (`File > Export Vector File`) | Export the layout view as PDF or SVG |

: The KLayout productivity plugins in a nutshell. {#tbl-klayout-plugins}

## Inspect / Edit the Layout {#sec-inspect-layout}

After the schematic is finalised and the design targets are met, the layout can be created. The layout of the `inverter` cell is hierarchical, and the top-level cell `inverter_top` contains four instances of the `inverter` cell. Around the 4-channel inverter layout, a power ring is drawn on `Metal5` and `TopMetal1` layers, which is connected to the `VDD` and `VSS` pins of the four inverters. This power ring is required for top-level integration, connecting the macro power to the chip's PDN.

With the following command, the GDS of the 4-channel inverter is opened in KLayout as shown in @fig-inverter-top-layout. Use the layer shortcuts `0`, `1`, `2`, ..., `9` from @tbl-klayout-plugins to view the individual layers.

```sh
ke layout/inverter_top.klay.gds
```

`inverter_top.klay.gds` is the source of truth. After modifying the layout, export a clean `.gds` file (for example `inverter_top.gds`) by pressing `File > Export Layout For Tapeout`, which resolves every PCell and library reference into a static cell so the result opens without the PDK loaded. Never hand-edit the exported file: keeping the two in step by editing both is how they drift apart, and the drift is invisible because the sign-off targets only look at the exported one. All verification flows (DRC, LVS, and PEX with both KLayout and Magic) accept either `.gds` or `.klay.gds`, while the build targets (LEF export, GDS copy, and rendering) use the exported `.gds`.

::: {.callout-warning}
The export re-evaluates the PCells against the **installed** PDK, so device geometry can change without anyone touching the layout, and the exported file is the only place that shows it. The sibling SG13CMOS5L template hit this for real: for the identical stored parameters its `SG13_dev` `pmos` draws the `NWell` (`31/0`) 0.11 µm tighter on every side than the geometry frozen into its exported GDS, which pulled the two mirrored pmos wells away from the hand-drawn `NWell` straps that bridge them and produced four `NW.b1` markers (min. PWell width between NWell regions) that no sign-off target saw. Measured on the 2026.08 container, this PDK still draws the wider well, so the two are not interchangeable: a layout carried between the templates has to be re-exported under the target PDK and re-checked, not copied. Re-run DRC, LVS and PEX after every export.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Never delete the box on the `prBoundary` layer (`189/0`) that frames the macro, and make sure a re-drawn layout still carries it. The chip flow derives the bounding box of every macro from this layer: Magic maps all datatypes of layer 189 to its boundary layer, and LibreLane's `Magic.StreamOut` step reads that boundary back for every macro it places. A layout without the box fails the whole chip build with `Failed to extract PR boundary from GDSII view of macro 'inverter_top'`, two flows away from the layout that caused it. Treat the box as part of the layout: keep it in the KLayout editing source `inverter_top.klay.gds` so every re-export carries it, and hide it at render time with `sak-render.py -x` if it spoils a chip shot. `make check-boundary` catches a missing box in the macro build, see @sec-build-deliverables.
:::

![`inverter_top` layout in KLayout.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_top_black.png){#fig-inverter-top-layout width=75%}

KLayout also supports a 2.5D viewer, which can be used to inspect the layout. To open the 2.5D viewer, press `SG13G2 PDK > BEOL 2.5D Viewer`. @fig-inverter-top-layout-3D shows the `inverter_top` layout in the 2.5D viewer.

![`inverter_top` layout in KLayout 2.5D viewer.](fig/inverter_top/inverter_top_3D.png){#fig-inverter-top-layout-3D width=100%}

### Drawing the `inverter` Unit Cell {#sec-draw-layout}

The hierarchy starts with the unit cell. [`layout/inverter.gds`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/layout/) is its editing source, and `inverter_top.klay.gds` pulls it in as a library through `inverter_top.klay.klib`, so the four instances follow every edit of the unit cell. To draw the unit cell from scratch, open KLayout with `ke` and go through the following steps. The finished result is the `inverter` cell inside @fig-inverter-top-layout.

1. **Create the cell.** `File > New Layout`, top cell name `inverter`, DBU $0.001\,\mathrm{\mu m}$.
2. **Place the transistor PCells.** Drag `nmos` and `pmos` from the `SG13_dev` library into the layout. Place the PMOS row above the NMOS row.
3. **Match the schematic.** Select each PCell and press `Q`. Set the same `w`, `l`, and `ng` values as in the schematic (@tbl-inverter-sizing-geom): the NMOS with $20 \times 1.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ fingers and the PMOS with $20 \times 6.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ fingers, both with $L = 1.0\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. As in the schematic, `w` is the total width that the PCell splits into `ng` fingers. Add the two dummy devices next to the active devices in the same way.
4. **Substrate and well contacts.** Tie the substrate to `VSS` and the n-well of the PMOS to `VDD` with `ptap1` / `ntap1` contacts (or a `guard_ring`).
5. **Route.** Connect the gates (input), the drains (output), and the source rails with `Metal1` and `Metal2`. Use the path tool `P`, place vias with `O` or with `via_stack` PCells. Keep signal routing on the lower metals within a macro. Use the layer shortcuts `1`, `2`, `8`, `9` to focus on the layer you are working on.
6. **Add the pins.** Select the target metal layer and press `Shift + P` to place the pins `vin`, `vout`, `VDD`, and `VSS`. The pin tool places the pin shape on `MetalX.pin` and the label on `MetalX.text`, which is exactly what LVS expects.
7. **Save** as `layout/inverter.gds`. Then open `inverter_top.klay.gds`, check the four instances and the power ring, and export `inverter_top.gds` as described above.

::: {.callout-tip}
The layout drawing order follows the matching rules of analog design: active devices in the centre with common orientation, dummies at the edges, and taps close to the devices. Also check the layout tips in the [KLayout cheatsheet](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/doc/klayout/klayout_cheatsheet.md).
:::

## DRC, LVS, and PEX

The inverter macro can be verified with two verification flows, either with KLayout or with Magic + Netgen. Each flow covers DRC, LVS, and PEX. Magic + Netgen provides only non-interactive command-line flows, while KLayout also has interactive GUI-based DRC and LVS.

### Design Rule Check

The non-interactive DRC can be run with the following Makefile targets (all three use `sak-drc.sh`). The `CELL` variable can be set to run DRC on a specific cell, or it defaults to `inverter_top` if not set. The `DRC_LEVEL` variable selects the KLayout DRC level and the gdscheck suite: `precheck`, `macro` (default), or `regular`. It is ignored by `magic-drc`, since Magic has no selectable rule decks and always runs the full rule set compiled into the PDK's Magic tech file.

| Check | `precheck` | `macro` _(default)_ | `regular` |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Foundry precheck rule set | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Pin / label | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Full FEOL + BEOL rules | – | ✓ | ✓ |
| Off-grid / angle | – | ✓ | ✓ |
| Recommended rules | – | ✓ | ✓ |
| Extra rules | – | – | ✓ |
| Density (full-chip fill) | – | – | ✓ |
| Antenna | – | – | ✓ |

```sh
make klayout-drc [CELL=<cellname>] [DRC_LEVEL=<precheck|macro|regular>] [DRC_JOBS=<n>]   # default CELL=inverter_top, default DRC_LEVEL=macro
make magic-drc [CELL=<cellname>]    # default CELL=inverter_top
make gdscheck-drc [CELL=<cellname>] [DRC_LEVEL=<precheck|macro|regular>] [GDSCHECK_SUITE=<suite>|GDSCHECK_DECKS=<decks>] [DRC_JOBS=<n>]   # default CELL=inverter_top
```

`DRC_JOBS` caps the number of KLayout processes of one run and sets the gdscheck threads. The default of 4 KLayout processes (fewer on a machine with fewer CPUs) and gdscheck on every CPU suits the macros, and larger values only pay off for the full chip on a server.

[gdscheck](https://github.com/aesc-silicon/gdscheck) is a standalone DRC engine with its own rule decks built into the binary. `DRC_LEVEL` maps onto its suites (`precheck` runs `precheck`, which includes the density rules, `macro` runs `core` and `regular` runs `main`), and `GDSCHECK_SUITE` replaces this mapping (`precheck`, `core`, `main`, `density`, `antenna` or `recommended`). `GDSCHECK_DECKS` runs single rule decks instead of a suite, comma-separated (for example `cont,via1`, `gdscheck list-decks --process ihp-sg13g2` lists them). The layer decks include their fill and density rules, so a single cell can fail a layer deck on a fill or density rule that `macro` does not check. Upstream calls gdscheck experimental, so it is a third opinion next to KLayout and Magic, not a sign-off, and the `make all` of the inverter runs it after the KLayout verification.

::: {.callout-note}
The `pmos` cell of the inverter is the `SG13_dev` `pmos` PCell with `guardRingType` set to `nwell`, which draws an nBuLay ring under its n+ tap ring. Magic reports `NBL.f` between that ring and the PMOS diffusion inside it and `NBL.d` against the NWell next to it, and gdscheck 0.2.0 reports `NBL.f`, while the KLayout deck passes the layout ([IHP-Open-PDK#954](https://github.com/IHP-GmbH/IHP-Open-PDK/issues/954), fixed in gdscheck after 0.2.0 by [aesc-silicon/gdscheck#51](https://github.com/aesc-silicon/gdscheck/pull/51)). KLayout is the sign-off deck. Until the fixes are in the container, `magic-drc` and `gdscheck-drc` fail on `inverter` and `inverter_top`, so the `make all` flows leave the Magic DRC out and stop at gdscheck until then.
:::

Reports are written into per-cell run folders (`<CELL>.magic.drc/` for Magic, `<CELL>.klayout.drc/` for KLayout, `<CELL>.gdscheck.drc/` for gdscheck) inside [`verification/drc/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/verification/drc/). The run folders are wiped at the start of each run, so they always reflect the latest run only.

A successful KLayout run ends with the line

```text
INFO    | KLayout DRC Check Passed: No DRC violations detected in the layout.
```

and a clean Magic report `<CELL>.magic.drc.rpt` lists `COUNT: 0` for the cell, which the inverter does not reach because of the guard ring markers above.

::: {.callout-tip}
In KLayout, a non-interactive DRC run can be launched from the GUI by pressing **`F9`**. The DRC options can be modified by pressing **`F10`**.

![KLayout DRC output windows.](fig/inverter_top/KLayout_DRC_Output.png){width=100%}
:::

### Layout-Versus-Schematic

The non-interactive LVS can be run with the following Makefile targets. The `CELL` variable can be set to run LVS on a specific cell, or it defaults to `inverter_top` if not set.

```sh
make klayout-lvs [CELL=<cellname>]  # default CELL=inverter_top, uses CDL netlist exported from Xschem
make magic-lvs [CELL=<cellname>]    # default CELL=inverter_top, uses SPICE netlist exported from Xschem
```

The schematic netlist is exported automatically by the matching `*-lvs-netlist` sub-target and moved to [`netlist/schematic/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/netlist/schematic/). The extracted layout netlist is moved to
[`netlist/layout/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/netlist/layout/) and the reports are written into per-cell run folders (`<CELL>.magic.lvs/` for Magic + Netgen, `<CELL>.klayout.lvs/` for KLayout) inside [`verification/lvs/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/verification/lvs/). The run folders are wiped at the start of each run, so they always reflect the latest run only.

Substrate and well contacts are not devices for LVS in either flow (KLayout skips the `ntap1` / `ptap1` device extraction, Magic extracts them as substrate connections), so the taps in the layout need no matching device in the schematic. A successful KLayout run prints:

```text
| Status           | PASS                                    |
| Mode             | COMPARE                                 |
| Outcome          | Comparison mode: PASS (netlists match). |
| Warnings         | 0                                       |
| Errors           | 0                                       |
```

The Magic + Netgen flow reports:

```text
Cell pin lists are equivalent.
Device classes inverter_top and inverter_top are equivalent.

Final result: Circuits match uniquely.
```

::: {.callout-note}
The Netgen report additionally states `Netlists match uniquely with property errors` and lists one warning per transistor about a `mm_ok` property that exists only on the schematic side. It is the mismatch switch of the Xschem symbol (see @sec-draw-schematic), which the layout PCell does not carry, so the two netlists cannot agree on it. This is expected with the current PDK and can be ignored as long as the final result reads `Circuits match uniquely.`
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
In KLayout, a non-interactive LVS run can be launched from the GUI by pressing **`F11`**. The LVS options can be modified by pressing **`F12`**, where the schematic netlist `inverter_top_klayout.cdl` has to be selected manually. Set `deep` as the run mode.

![KLayout LVS output windows.](fig/inverter_top/KLayout_LVS_Output.png){width=100%}
:::

### Parasitic Extraction {#sec-pex}

The non-interactive PEX can be run with the following Makefile targets. The `CELL` variable can be set to run PEX on a specific cell, or it defaults to `inverter_top` if not set. The `EXT_MODE` variable can be set to choose between different extraction modes,

- `EXT_MODE=1` for C-decoupled mode,
- `EXT_MODE=2` for C-coupled mode,
- `EXT_MODE=3` for full-RC extraction.

If not set, it defaults to `EXT_MODE=3`.

For full-RC extraction (`EXT_MODE=3`), `magic-pex` also exposes the `sak-pex.sh` `extresist` tuning parameters (ignored in `EXT_MODE=1`/`2`):

- `THRESHOLD` - extresist threshold in mOhm (`-t`, default `10000` = 10 Ohm),
- `MINRES` - extresist minimum resistance in mOhm (`-r`, default `1000` = 1 Ohm),
- `MINDELAY` - extresist minimum delay in ps (`-y`, default `1`; `0` = gate by resistance).

```sh
make klayout-pex [CELL=<cellname>] [EXT_MODE=<1|2|3>]   # default CELL=inverter_top, default EXT_MODE=3 (full-RC)
make magic-pex [CELL=<cellname>] [EXT_MODE=<1|2|3>] [THRESHOLD=<mOhm>] [MINRES=<mOhm>] [MINDELAY=<ps>]   # default CELL=inverter_top, default EXT_MODE=3 (full-RC)
```

PEX writes a SPICE netlist into [`netlist/pex/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/netlist/pex/). The subcircuit is named `<CELL>_pex`, and the pin order is rearranged to match the Xschem PEX symbol ([`inverter_top_pex.sym`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/schematic/xschem/inverter_top_pex.sym)).

That PEX symbol is generated, not maintained by hand. Both PEX targets start by running `make symbol-pex`, which copies `schematic/xschem/<CELL>.sym` to `schematic/xschem/<CELL>_pex.sym` and changes `type=subcircuit` into `type=primitive`. Everything else is inherited, above all the pin order that `sak-pin-reorder.py` sorts the extracted netlist to. The `primitive` type keeps Xschem from descending into a schematic of the same name, so the instance is netlisted as it stands and its subcircuit comes from the included PEX netlist instead. Because the symbol is rebuilt before every extraction, it cannot go stale when a pin is added, removed or renamed, and it can be built on its own with `make symbol-pex [CELL=<cellname>]`. Edit `<CELL>.sym`, never the generated `<CELL>_pex.sym`.

After the reorder, both PEX targets run [`scripts/check_pex_ports.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/scripts/check_pex_ports.py) on the extracted netlist and fail if a port of the subcircuit is not connected to any element inside it. A floating port usually means a missing or misspelled pin label in the layout, and it is better caught here than as a silently open input in the post-layout simulation.

::: {.callout-note}
Every symbol in this template carries `spectre_format="@name ( @pinlist ) @symname"` next to its `format` line. Xschem writes that line itself whenever a symbol is generated from a schematic's pin list (key `a`), and only the Spectre netlister reads it, which is also the one that drives VACASK. The SPICE netlister used for Ngspice ignores it. Do not delete it: without it, instances of that symbol are silently dropped from a Spectre/VACASK netlist and its `subckt` line comes out with an empty port list, with no warning at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Note that [KLayout-PEX (KPEX)](https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex) is currently under development and therefore the Magic engine is used internally for the actual extraction.
:::

### Post-Layout Simulation {#sec-postlayout}

Now we close the loop and simulate the extracted layout in the same testbenches. Every testbench already carries a spare instance of the PEX symbol (`x3`, see @sec-tb-ac), and the PEX symbol has the same pin positions as the cell symbol, so the swap takes a few key presses:

1. Open a testbench, for example `inverter_tb_ac_ol.sch`.
2. Select the active instance `x1` (`inverter.sym`) and press `Shift + T` to set its `spice_ignore` flag. It is now excluded from the netlist.
3. Select the spare instance `x3` (`inverter_pex.sym`), move it with `m` onto the position of `x1`, and press `Shift + T` to activate it. Its pins land on the same wires, so nothing else changes.
4. The `.include ../../../netlist/pex/inverter_magic_pex_3.spice` line at the top of the control block now supplies the subcircuit definition. If you extracted with a different `EXT_MODE` or with KLayout, adapt the file name (for example `inverter_klayout_pex_3.spice`).
5. Re-run the simulation with `Ctrl` + click on **Simulate**.

The same swap works in `inverter_top_tb_tran.sch` with `inverter_top_pex.sym` and `inverter_top_magic_pex_3.spice`, which is the post-layout view that `make all` refreshes before it simulates (see @sec-full-analog-flow).

Compare the post-layout results against the schematic-level results. What differences do you see, and why?

Think about it before simulating. The extracted netlist adds the wiring resistance and the capacitance of every drawn wire to the circuit. The dc transfer characteristic should barely change, because almost no current flows into the parasitics at dc. In the ac response, the added output and internal capacitances and the interconnect resistance shift the poles, so expect a slightly reduced bandwidth and small changes in the measured gain. If your post-layout results deviate strongly, that is usually a sign of a layout problem, for example a too narrow or too long wire on a critical net.

### Run Full Verification Flow at Once

If you want to run the full verification flow at once, the verify targets bundle DRC, LVS, and PEX with KLayout and LVS and PEX with Magic in one command.

```sh
make klayout-verify [CELL=<cellname>]   # default CELL=inverter_top
make magic-verify [CELL=<cellname>]     # default CELL=inverter_top
```

`magic-verify` leaves the Magic DRC out until the fixes for the guard ring markers described above are in the container, `make magic-drc` runs it on its own. gdscheck has no LVS or PEX, so it is not part of these bundles. Run it with `make gdscheck-drc [CELL=<cellname>]`, or with `make gdscheck-drc-all` for `inverter` and `inverter_top`.

## Build Deliverables for Top-Level Integration {#sec-build-deliverables}

For the inverter to be picked up by the top-level LibreLane flow, it must expose a **[LEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LEF/DEF)** (abstract pin / blockage view), a **[Liberty timing library](https://chipverify.com/rtl-synthesis/introduction-to-liberty-format)** stub, and a **Verilog stub**. The Verilog stub is referenced by [`rtl/chip_top.sv`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/rtl/chip_top.sv) for top-level integration. These files can be built with individual Makefile targets or via `build-top`.

```sh
make check-boundary   # check the PR boundary box on layer 189 in layout/inverter_top.gds
make lef              # final/lef/inverter_top.lef
make lib              # final/lib/inverter_top.lib
make verilog          # final/vh/inverter_top.vh
make build-top        # the four steps above plus copy-gds and render-gds
```

`make build-top` runs `check-boundary` first, so a top cell without the PR boundary box fails the macro build in a second with a message that names the layer, instead of failing the chip flow much later (see the callout in @sec-inspect-layout). The check runs [`scripts/check_boundary.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/inverter/scripts/check_boundary.py), which also reports the size of the box and warns when the drawn geometry extends beyond it, because the top-level flow places the macro by the boundary and anything outside it may overlap a neighbour.

`make build-top` also copies the GDS to [`final/gds/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/final/gds/) and renders the macro to [`render/img/inverter_top_white.png` and `render/img/inverter_top_black.png`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/inverter/render/img/), as displayed in @fig-inverter-top-layout.

## Full Analog Macro Flow {#sec-full-analog-flow}

The full verification, build, and simulation chain is run with the following command.

```sh
make all
```

This calls `klayout-verify-all`, `gdscheck-drc-all`, `magic-verify-all`, `build-top`, and `sim-all` (Xschem + CACE) in sequence. The simulations run last, so the `inverter_top` testbench includes the PEX netlist produced by this run. Depending on the hardware used, a full pass can take a few minutes, especially the CACE simulation step.


# RF Macro Implementation {#sec-rf}

The [`vco`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/) macro is the RF reference macro of the template: a 20 GHz LC voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) built from CMOS devices only. It follows the analog flow of @sec-analog (Xschem, DRC, LVS and PEX with KLayout and Magic) and adds the steps an RF block needs on top:

- **Layouts from scripts.** Every layout is written by a KLayout Python script (@sec-rf-layout).
- **EM simulation of the passives.** The tank coil is simulated with [AWS Palace](https://github.com/awslabs/palace), set up from its layout by [gds2palace](https://github.com/VolkerMuehlhaus/gds2palace_ihp_sg13g2) (@sec-rf-em).
- **Lumped-element models.** [snp2le](https://github.com/iic-jku/snp2le) turns the S-parameters of the EM simulation into netlists for ngspice and VACASK (@sec-rf-snp2le).
- **Large-signal RF analyses.** [VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK) computes the S-parameters of the coil model (ACSP), the periodic steady state of the oscillator (PSS), its phase noise (PNOISE) and its tuning gain (PAC) (@sec-rf-sim).
- **Post-layout simulation at 20 GHz.** The extracted netlist of the macro is simulated with the EM model of the coil in place: the start-up over corners (@sec-rf-corners), the power-up and the enable (@sec-rf-powerup), and the phase noise from transient noise (@sec-rf-trannoise).

The VCO is a simple design to learn the RF flow on, not an optimized one. It goes through each step once, and the [vco README](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/README.md) lists where it falls short and what a better design would change.

::: {.callout-note}
The VCO is not part of the chip top-level yet. Its integration needs a quiet analog pad of its own for the macro's `VDD`, RF pads or a divider for the 20 GHz output, and a gap in the chip power grid, since the coil occupies both TopMetal layers. The open steps are listed under [Open Points](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/README.md#open-points) in the README.
:::

## Circuit {#sec-rf-circuit}

The core follows a published design, the 27 GHz cross-coupled VCO of Jung and Park ([Electronics Letters, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1049/el:20080527)), scaled to 20 GHz and to the devices of this PDK. @fig-vco-top-schematic shows the macro and @tbl-vco-cells its cells. It needs four pins besides its outputs: the supply `VDD`, `VSS`, the enable `di_en` and the tuning voltage `vtune`.

| Cell | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `vco_top` | the macro: bias, tap feed, core and buffer, and the pins |
| `vco_core` | LC tank and negative resistance: the coil, the cross-coupled NMOS pair, the varactor array, and the decoupling capacitors of the center tap `vdd_core` |
| `vco_ind` | the center-tapped tank coil: the PDK `inductor3` for LVS, the lumped-element model `vco_ind_le` for simulation |
| `vco_var` | the varactor array: three `sg13_hv_svaricap`, gates on the tank, wells on `vtune` |
| `vco_buf` | AC-coupled differential output buffer with 50 $\Omega$ back-termination |
| `vco_feed` | the feed of the center tap from `VDD`: the switch `MPs` and the resistor `Rct` |
| `vco_bias` | the 100 $\mu$A reference from `VDD`, the enable logic, the two bias voltages of the buffer, each behind an RC low-pass filter, and the RF decoupling of `vbg_buf` |

: Cells of the `vco` macro. {#tbl-vco-cells tbl-colwidths="[15,85]"}

![Schematic of `vco_top`: bias (top), tap feed, LC core and output buffer.](fig/vco_top/vco_top_schematic.svg){#fig-vco-top-schematic}

The core in @fig-vco-core-schematic has no current source. The center tap of the coil hangs on a resistor from `VDD` (@fig-vco-feed-schematic), so it finds its own voltage, 0.76 V post-layout, which sets the common mode of the tank and the gate-source voltage of the pair at once, and with it the current and the amplitude. A slow corner draws less current, so the tap rises and gives the pair more gate voltage, a fast corner the other way round. The varactors sit with their gates on the tank and their wells on `vtune`, so a tuning voltage from 0 V to `VDD` = 1.5 V sweeps them across their capacitance transition around 0 V gate-to-well voltage. A differential pair buffers the tank into two outputs with 50 $\Omega$ back-termination. `di_en` low opens the switch of the tap and of the reference, so the core, the buffer and the bias stop. The [Circuit](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/README.md#circuit) section of the README explains the sizing and why the design ended up this way.

![Schematic of `vco_core`: the coil `vco_ind`, the varactor array `vco_var`, the cross-coupled pair `M1`/`M2` and the decoupling capacitors `Cct1`/`Cct2` of the center tap.](fig/vco_top/vco_core_schematic.svg){#fig-vco-core-schematic}

![Schematic of `vco_feed`: the switch `MPs` (96 $\mu$m / 0.13 $\mu$m) and `Rct` (17.3 $\mu$m by 8.8 $\mu$m of `rppd`) from `VDD` to the center tap.](fig/vco_top/vco_feed_schematic.svg){#fig-vco-feed-schematic width=60%}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why a Resistor and Not a Current Source
A current source on the center tap sets the tank's common mode by the pair's gate-source voltage at a fixed current, so the noise of the bias moves the varactors' operating point, and with it the frequency. A PMOS mirror from `VDD` in place of `Rct` gives -98.3 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz behind a 190 k$\Omega$ and 10 pF filter and -88.8 dBc/Hz without one, against -101.3 dBc/Hz with the resistor. The resistor has its own price: noise on `VDD` reaches the tap and the frequency, so the macro's `VDD` needs a quiet pad of its own.
:::

| Parameter | Target | Schematic | Post-layout |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Oscillation frequency at `vtune` = 0.75 V | 20 GHz | 22.55 GHz | 20.00 GHz |
| Tuning range, `vtune` from 0 V to 1.5 V | about 2 GHz | 21.64 GHz to 24.04 GHz | 19.34 GHz to 21.18 GHz |
| Phase noise at 1 MHz offset | reported | -101.2 dBc/Hz (PNOISE), -99.4 dBc/Hz (transient noise) | -101.5 dBc/Hz (PNOISE), -101.1 dBc/Hz (transient noise) |
| Output power per output into 50 $\Omega$ | -10 dBm or more | -8.3 dBm | -10.0 dBm |
| Supply current from `VDD` = 1.5 V | | 11.6 mA | 10.9 mA |
| Disabled | | | 9 nA, no oscillation |

: Results of the `vco` at TT and 27 C. The schematic frequency is from the PSS, the post-layout one from the transient of @sec-rf-postlayout, and both output powers are the fundamental from the PSS. {#tbl-vco-results}

## Directory Structure {#sec-rf-dirs}

The design files are located in [`macros/vco/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/). The folders of the inverter are all there (@sec-analog), plus the ones for the layout scripts and the EM simulation:

| Folder | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| [`schematic/xschem/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/schematic/xschem/) | Schematics and symbols of the seven cells, the generated PEX symbols, and `vco_ind_le.sym` for the coil model. |
| [`scripts/layout/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/scripts/layout/) | One KLayout Python script per cell and the shared helpers `vco_layout.py`. |
| [`layout/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/layout/) | The GDS of every cell, written by its script. |
| [`scripts/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/scripts/) | The checks of the inverter, the post-layout extraction helpers `drop_subcells.py`, `pex_caps.py` and `spice2spectre.py`, and the scripted runs `sim_corners.py`, `sim_powerup.py` and `sim_trannoise.py`. |
| [`verification/em/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/verification/em/) | `scripts/palace_vco_ind.py` (the EM setup), `layout/` (the EM layout with its ports), `palace_model/` (the Palace configuration and results) and `s-parameter/` (the Touchstone file the model is fitted to). |
| [`netlist/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/netlist/) | `schematic/`, `layout/` and `pex/` as in the inverter, plus the coil model for ngspice (`spice/vco_ind_le.spice`) and for VACASK (`spectre/vco_ind_le.inc`), and the post-layout netlist for VACASK (`spectre/vco_top_leads.inc`). |
| [`testbenches/xschem/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/testbenches/xschem/) | The ngspice and VACASK testbenches, the post-layout wrapper `vco_top_lpe.sch`, a patched model file in `models/`, and the plot scripts in `plot_simulations/`. |
| [`verification/drc/`, `verification/lvs/`, `final/`, `render/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/) | Reports, deliverables and renders, as in the inverter. |

The [Makefile](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/Makefile) has every target of the inverter and adds the RF steps. @tbl-rf-flow lists the flow in the order of its steps.

| Step | Tools | Make target | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Layout generation | KLayout Python | `klayout-script`, `klayout-script-all` | `layout/` |
| DRC | KLayout, gdscheck, Magic | `klayout-drc`, `klayout-drc-regular`, `gdscheck-drc`, `magic-drc` | `verification/drc/` |
| LVS | Xschem, KLayout, Magic, Netgen | `klayout-lvs`, `magic-lvs` | `verification/lvs/`, `netlist/schematic/`, `netlist/layout/` |
| PEX | KPEX, Magic | `klayout-pex-leads`, `klayout-pex`, `magic-pex` | `netlist/pex/`, `netlist/spectre/` |
| EM simulation | gds2palace, AWS Palace | `sim-em` | `verification/em/layout/`, `verification/em/palace_model/` |
| S-parameters | | `copy-sparam`, `view-em-sim` | `verification/em/s-parameter/` |
| Lumped-element model | snp2le | `snp2le`, `em-model` | `netlist/spice/`, `netlist/spectre/` |
| Circuit simulation | Xschem, ngspice, VACASK | `sim-xschem`, `sim-all`, `sim-corners` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/` |
| Post-layout tuning curve | ngspice | `sim-tune-lpe` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/figures/` |
| Power-up and enable | ngspice | `sim-powerup` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/` |
| Transient noise | VACASK | `sim-trannoise`, `sim-trannoise-lpe` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data/` |
| Post-layout PSS | VACASK | `sim-pss-lpe` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data/` |
| Plots | Python | `sim-view-xschem` | `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/figures/` |
| Deliverables | Magic, `sak-render.py` | `build-top` | `final/`, `render/img/` |
| Everything but EM and the long runs | all of the above | `all` | |

: Flow steps of the `vco` and their Makefile targets. {#tbl-rf-flow tbl-colwidths="[20,22,30,28]"}

`make all` runs `klayout-script-all`, `klayout-verify-all`, `gdscheck-drc-all`, `magic-verify-all`, `build-top` and `sim-all`, in about 28 minutes on a compute host. It leaves out the EM simulation of the coil, which takes 35 minutes on a compute host, the corners, and the two long runs: the power-up transient and the transient noise take hours each. Their results are committed, so `make all` simulates with the coil model of the last EM run.

## Layout Generation {#sec-rf-layout}

A layout can be drawn by hand, generated by a parametric library, or written as a script. This template and its RF sibling [SPARX](https://github.com/iic-jku/SG13CMOS_SPARX) have an example of each:

| Method | Example | Strong at | Weak at |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hand drawing in KLayout | the `inverter` (@sec-draw-layout) | full control, learning the rules, small cells | every change is manual, and a GDS diff shows nothing a reviewer can read |
| GDSFactory generator | the SPARX receiver | parametric passives, a whole chip from a few design inputs | a structure needs a generator before it can be drawn |
| KLayout Python scripts written by an AI coding agent | the `vco` | a design in review: every change is a script diff, and every layout is rebuilt in seconds | the agent sees the layout through DRC, LVS and PEX only, so the designer reviews it in KLayout |

: Three ways to a layout. {#tbl-layout-methods tbl-colwidths="[24,20,28,28]"}

### Drawing by Hand

Hand drawing works for RF cells as it does for the inverter in @sec-draw-layout. Place the PDK's `inductor3` PCell from the `SG13_dev` library for a coil, set its parameters with `Q`, route it, and export the layout with `File > Export Layout For Tapeout`. Three rules matter more at RF than in an analog cell:

- **Keep the coil's keep-out free.** The PCell draws a keep-out of the outer diameter plus 60 $\mu$m with the `IND` layer and the no-fill layers, so no fill lands under or next to the windings. Keep the other circuits out of it as well.
- **Close no loop around the coil.** A closed ring of metal around a coil, a guard ring or a supply ring, carries the induced eddy current and lowers its inductance and its Q.
- **Short and wide leads.** At 20 GHz, the lead from the coil to the transistors is part of the tank, see @sec-rf-postlayout.

### Programmatic Layout with GDSFactory

[GDSFactory](https://github.com/gdsfactory/gdsfactory) is a Python library for parametric layouts. The [IHP-GDSFactory-Addon](https://github.com/iic-jku/IHP-GDSFactory-Addon) wraps the PCells and the layer stack of the IHP Open-PDK for it, and adds a library of RF structures: transmission lines and corners, the branch-line coupler, the Wilkinson power divider, coupled-line and hairpin bandpass filters, a directional coupler and a quarter-wave transformer.

SPARX, a 160 GHz six-port receiver, is built that way. Its generator takes the design frequency as the only design input, computes every line width and length from closed-form models, and writes the complete chip with fill, pads and seal ring, together with the EM sub-structures and their port markers. The EM simulation therefore always solves the structures that are in the chip.

```sh
make build-layout            # the 160 GHz chip
make build-layout FREQ=77    # the same receiver for 77 GHz
```

The [Programmatic Layout Generation](https://iic-jku.github.io/SG13CMOS_SPARX/#sec-layout) chapter of the SPARX documentation explains the generator, and its [Design Flow](https://iic-jku.github.io/SG13CMOS_SPARX/#sec-flow) chapter the Makefile targets around it.

### KLayout Python Scripts Written by an AI Coding Agent

Every layout of the `vco` is a KLayout Python script in [`scripts/layout/`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/tree/main/macros/vco/scripts/layout/), run in batch mode, which writes `layout/<CELL>.gds`. Nothing is drawn by hand: to change a layout, change its script, rerun it, and rerun DRC and LVS.

```sh
make klayout-script CELL=vco_ind   # klayout -b -r scripts/layout/vco_ind.py
make klayout-script-all            # every cell, subcells before the cells that place them
```

The scripts use the Python API of KLayout (`pya`) and the PCells of the PDK. The coil, for example, is the `inductor3` PCell with its pin labels, shortened from [`vco_ind.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/scripts/layout/vco_ind.py):

```python
ly = pya.Layout()
ly.dbu = 0.001
top = ly.create_cell("vco_ind")
# subE=0, not False: the PCell draws the backside etch layer LBE for the boolean False
ind = ly.create_cell("inductor3", "SG13_dev", {"w": "4u", "s": "4u", "d": "52u", "nr_r": 2, "subE": 0})
top.insert(pya.CellInstArray(ind.cell_index(), pya.Trans()))
top.flatten(-1, True)                    # no PCell context left in the GDS
for text, (layer, datatype), x, y in LABELS:
    top.shapes(ly.layer(layer, datatype)).insert(pya.DText(text, x, y))
ly.write(out_file, opt)
```

The scripts of the larger cells place transistors, resistors and capacitors from the PDK's `SG13_dev` library and route them with the helpers of [`vco_layout.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/scripts/layout/vco_layout.py), which build a transistor with its wiring, snap every coordinate to the 5 nm grid, merge each metal into one polygon per connected piece, and check every DC path against the current limits of the process (@sec-rf-current-density).

These scripts were written by an AI coding agent that ran the flow in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container. It worked from the schematic, a floorplan and the rules of the template: it wrote a script, ran it, ran DRC and LVS, read the reports, and changed the script until both were clean. The designer reviewed the layout in KLayout and the script as a diff. The loop works because every step is a Make target that writes a text report. What it does not replace is the review: a layout that passes DRC and LVS can still be a poor RF layout. The first core of this macro joined the source bar of the pair to `VSS` through one via stack, and only the post-layout netlist showed the 14.7 $\Omega$ in series with the core current (@sec-rf-postlayout).

::: {.callout-tip}
## What the Scripts Had to Learn
Some of the traps the agent ran into are worth knowing for any KLayout script:

- A KLayout batch script that ends in `SystemExit` exits with code 0 and prints nothing, so a failed check leaves the old GDS in place. Raise `RuntimeError` instead, which KLayout reports and `make` stops on.
- PDK PCells write their terminal names as texts (`inductor3` its `LA`, `LB` and `LC`). KLayout LVS names a net after each text, and a net with a second name fails the strict port check. Repeat the PCell's names in the pin labels, or drop the texts once the cell is flat.
- The resistor and MIM PCells compute a dimension from R or C by default. Pass `Calculate="R"` and `Calculate="C"` to keep the drawn width and length.
- KLayout LVS does not combine parallel devices (`m`) with a multi-finger device, so a transistor drawn as one device with 30 fingers is `ng=30` in the schematic.
- A metal line that touches the first source stripe of a transistor can short a net that DRC cannot see. Here the enable line of the tap's switch did, and only LVS found it.
:::

@fig-vco-top-layout shows the result. The coil and its keep-out take 60 % of the 143 $\mu$m by 215.5 $\mu$m macro, and the core's tank lines run straight down from the coil's feeds to the pair and the varactors below. The bias sits on the left, the decoupling capacitors of the center tap on the right, the buffer under the core and the tap feed in the bottom right corner, next to the supply straps along the bottom edge. The [Generate the Layouts](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/README.md#generate-the-layouts-with-klayout-python-scripts) section of the README describes the floorplan of every cell.

![Layout of `vco_top`, written by the KLayout Python scripts, annotated: the coil at the top, below it the core's column with the pair and the varactor array, the buffer at the bottom, the bias on the left, the decoupling capacitors on the right and the tap feed in the bottom right corner. The render ends at the coil's top turn.](fig/vco_top/vco_top_annotated.png){#fig-vco-top-layout}

## DRC, LVS and PEX {#sec-rf-verify}

The verification targets are those of the inverter, see @sec-analog: `klayout-drc`, `gdscheck-drc`, `magic-drc`, `klayout-lvs`, `magic-lvs`, `klayout-pex`, `magic-pex` and the `*-verify` targets, all with `CELL=<cellname>`. What differs is which check can run on which cell:

| Cell | KLayout | gdscheck | Magic |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `vco_bias`, `vco_buf`, `vco_feed` | DRC, LVS | DRC | LVS, PEX |
| `vco_var`, `vco_ind`, `vco_core` | DRC, LVS | DRC | |
| `vco_top` | DRC, regular DRC, LVS, PEX without the coil and the varactor array (`klayout-pex-leads`) | DRC | PEX for the pin list of the Verilog stub |

: Checks per cell, as `klayout-verify-all`, `gdscheck-drc-all` and `magic-verify-all` run them. {#tbl-vco-checks}

The gaps have three reasons:

- **Magic extracts the varactor as two two-terminal halves** and does not extract the PDK inductor, so Netgen cannot compare a cell that holds either.
- **KPEX cannot read Magic's extraction of the varactor**, which Magic writes as a Verilog-A device. Every cell above the array inherits it.
- **An RC extraction of a coil is not its RF model.** It misses the inductance and the coupling: KPEX turns `vco_ind` into a single 42 fF capacitor. The model of the coil is its EM simulation, see @sec-rf-em.

The KLayout `macro` level of `klayout-drc` leaves out the density rules, and with them rules a macro has to meet on its own, such as the minimum metal areas `Mn.d` and `pSD.b`. So `klayout-verify-all` also runs `klayout-drc-regular` on `vco_top`, which fails on any rule but the global densities that only the chip's fill can meet.

The Magic DRC stays out of the flows, as in the inverter: `magic-drc` reports `LU.d` and `Cnt.a` on `sg13_hv_svaricap` and `MIM.e` and `Slt.c` on `cap_cmim`. A bare PCell of each, with none of this macro's wiring, reports the same rules and KLayout passes them, so they belong to the PDK's cells or Magic's rule deck and get fixed upstream.

### Current Density {#sec-rf-current-density}

No DRC deck checks electromigration, so the layout scripts do. Every DC path of the macro, each wire and each via array, is held against the limits of the process for 11 years at 105 C, for example 2 mA per $\mu$m of width on Metal2 to Metal5 and 0.4 mA per cut of Via1 to Via4:

```python
check_wire("drain plate of MPs", "Metal3", width, I_CORE)
check_cuts("tap's stack, top", "TopVia1", n_cuts, I_CORE)
```

The currents are the highest of the post-layout corners at that temperature, FF with the strong resistor corner and `VDD` at 1.65 V: 5.9 mA in the core and 7.6 mA in the buffer's tail. A script prints the ratio of each path and stops above 1, so a layout that would wear out does not get written. The highest ratio is 0.76, on the drain plate of the tap's switch. Two things came out of it: a source stripe at the finger pitch of a short transistor cannot be wider than 0.16 $\mu$m on Metal1, so those transistors carry a Metal2 strip over every source stripe, and the macro's `VDD` strap moved from 2 $\mu$m of Metal4, rated for 4 mA, to TopMetal1.

### Parasitic Extraction at 20 GHz

The post-layout netlist of the macro comes from `klayout-pex-leads`: one extraction of `vco_top` without the coil and the varactor array, which have models of their own.

```sh
make klayout-pex-leads   # netlist/pex/vco_top_leads_klayout_pex_3.spice and netlist/spectre/vco_top_leads.inc
```

- [`drop_subcells.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/scripts/drop_subcells.py) writes `vco_top` without the two subcells and puts a port where each of their pins lands on the remaining metal. The coil model and the varactor array then attach where they really connect, and the extraction keeps all the wiring between them and the pins of the macro.
- **The full-RC thresholds are ten times finer than in the inverter**: `THRESHOLD=1000` (1 $\Omega$), `MINRES=100` (0.1 $\Omega$) and `MINDELAY=0`. At the defaults, every net except `VSS` came out without resistance, the tank leads included. With the coil's own 2.4 $\Omega$ per side, a lead of 1 $\Omega$ is part of the tank.
- **The capacitances come from a C-coupled run of the same layout.** Magic's resistance extraction counts the coupling capacitance of a net with a resistor network a second time ([magic#557](https://github.com/RTimothyEdwards/magic/issues/557)), so [`pex_caps.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/scripts/pex_caps.py) keeps the resistors and devices of the full-RC run and scales its capacitors to the totals of the C-coupled run.
- [`spice2spectre.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/scripts/spice2spectre.py) translates the netlist for VACASK, for the post-layout transient noise (@sec-rf-trannoise).

The [Parasitic Extraction (PEX)](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/README.md#parasitic-extraction-pex) section of the README covers the details, among them a net without a resistor network and why the extraction runs in KPEX and not in `sak-pex.sh`.

## EM Simulation of RF Passives {#sec-rf-em}

At 20 GHz, the coil is the tank. Its inductance sets the frequency, and its loss sets the swing and the phase noise. Both depend on how the current flows in the windings (skin and proximity effect), on the eddy currents in the substrate, and on the capacitance between the turns and to the substrate. An RC extraction sees none of this, and the PDK has no SPICE model of its `inductor3`. A 3D field solver does: it solves Maxwell's equations on a mesh of the layout and returns the S-parameters of the structure at its ports.

The open-source flow for the IHP Open-PDK uses two tools:

- [**gds2palace**](https://github.com/VolkerMuehlhaus/gds2palace_ihp_sg13g2) by Volker Mühlhaus reads the GDS, the process stackup of the PDK (an XML file in `libs.tech/palace/`) and the port markers, and writes the mesh and the solver configuration.
- [**AWS Palace**](https://github.com/awslabs/palace) solves it with the finite element method in the frequency domain, in parallel with MPI. An adaptive frequency sweep solves the full model at a few frequencies only and fills in the rest from a reduced-order model.

The same flow simulates any planar passive: inductors and transformers, MIM and MoM capacitors, microstrip lines, filters, branch-line couplers and power dividers. SPARX simulates its couplers, its divider, its filter and its complete seven-port core at 160 GHz, see the [EM Simulation](https://iic-jku.github.io/SG13CMOS_SPARX/#sec-em) chapter of its documentation for the settings, the metal models and the cost.

### The EM Simulation of the Coil

```sh
make sim-em        # EM layout, Palace model, solve, Touchstone files
make copy-sparam   # copy the result to verification/em/s-parameter/vco_ind.s3p
make view-em-sim   # plot L, Q and the S-parameters
make em-model      # sim-em, copy-sparam, snp2le and the ACSP testbench in one go
make sim-em NP=8   # more MPI processes
```

`sim-em` runs [`palace_vco_ind.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/verification/em/scripts/palace_vco_ind.py), which reads `layout/vco_ind.gds` and builds the EM layout of @fig-vco-ind-em-layout: the coil metals, a Metal1 ground frame half a coil diameter away from the windings, a ground tongue under the feeds, and three 50 $\Omega$ lumped ports as vertical sheets from the tongue up to the pins. The script reads the diameter and the pins from the layout, so it follows a change of the coil. From that layout and the settings of @tbl-vco-em-settings, gds2palace writes the Palace model, Palace solves it, and the PDK's `combine_extend_snp.py` writes the Touchstone file `vco_ind.s3p`.

![EM layout of the coil: TopMetal2 windings, TopMetal1 underpass and feeds, the Metal1 ground frame and the three lumped ports in the order of snp2le's center-tapped coil model.](fig/vco_top/vco_ind_em_layout.svg){#fig-vco-ind-em-layout width=70%}

| Setting | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Process stackup | `SG13G2_200um.xml` of the PDK, with its 200 $\mu$m lossy substrate |
| Ports | three 50 $\Omega$ lumped ports at `LA`, `LB` and the center tap `LC` |
| Metal model | volume: the current is solved inside the metal, via arrays merged into blocks with their resistance corrected (`fill_factor_correction`) |
| Mesh | 2 $\mu$m cells in TopMetal1 and TopMetal2 |
| Element order | 3 |
| Frequency sweep | 0 Hz to 60 GHz in 0.75 GHz steps (gds2palace replaces 0 Hz by 10 MHz and 20 MHz), adaptive, to cover the third harmonic |
| Cost | 35 minutes and 9.8 GB with `NP=16` on a compute host |

: Palace settings of the coil. {#tbl-vco-em-settings tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

::: {.callout-important}
## Check the EM Result Against Something You Can Calculate
gds2palace models a metal either as a hollow shell with a surface impedance on every face (its default) or as a solid volume. The coil's traces are 4 $\mu$m wide and 2 $\mu$m to 3 $\mu$m thick, where the surface model is least accurate. The DC resistance shows which model is right, because it follows from the drawn lengths and the sheet resistances of the stackup by hand. For the first coil of this macro, the traces and the via fields add up to 2.8 $\Omega$. The volume model gave 2.93 $\Omega$ at 10 MHz, the surface model 1.65 $\Omega$, less than the traces alone, and a Q 46 % too high at 20 GHz. Check the mesh the same way: a finer mesh or a higher element order has to leave the result unchanged. Going from second to third order changed the Q of this coil by 2.3 % at 20 GHz.
:::

## Lumped-Element Models with snp2le {#sec-rf-snp2le}

A circuit simulator does not read S-parameters in a transient or a PSS. [snp2le](https://github.com/iic-jku/snp2le) turns a Touchstone file into a lumped-element netlist for both simulators of the flow, `netlist/spice/<name>.spice` for ngspice and `netlist/spectre/<name>.inc` for VACASK. It has two modes:

- **Universal.** A vector fit of the S-parameters with [scikit-rf](https://scikit-rf.org), synthesized into resistors, capacitors and controlled sources, with passivity enforced. It works for any structure and any number of ports, but its elements have no physical meaning. Its resistors are therefore noiseless, and `--thermal-noise` adds the thermal noise the passive really has.
- **Structure-specific.** A physical topology fitted to the data, so every element maps to the structure: `inductor-pi`, `inductor-wideband` and `inductor-ct` for coils, `mim-cap` for MIM and MoM capacitors, `tline-rlgc` for transmission lines, and models of the Wilkinson divider, the branch-line coupler and the balun. Its resistors are the loss of the structure and carry their thermal noise.

```sh
make snp2le                                                         # inductor-ct fit of verification/em/s-parameter/vco_ind.s3p
make snp2le EM=<structure> SNP=<file.sNp> LE_MODEL=universal ORDER=8
```

The coil uses `inductor-ct`, the wideband model of a center-tapped coil: two coupled half coils with their skin effect and substrate network, fitted over the whole band of the EM data. The file stem, the `.SUBCKT` name and the name of the symbol are the same (`vco_ind_le`), so a new fit drops into the schematic without an edit. The SPARX documentation explains both modes, the passivity enforcement and the noise in its [snp2le](https://iic-jku.github.io/SG13CMOS_SPARX/#sec-snp2le) chapter.

`vco_ind.sch` holds two views of the coil. The PDK's `inductor3` is what KLayout LVS compares with the layout, and every simulation netlist skips it. The model `vco_ind_le` is what the simulations use, and the LVS netlist skips it. The testbench `vco_ind_tb_acsp_vacask` checks the model against the EM data with VACASK's S-parameter analysis (ACSP), @fig-vco-ind-acsp. From 1.5 GHz to 40 GHz the model is within 2.9 % of the EM inductance and within 3.7 % of its Q, and at 20.25 GHz it gives 427 pH and a Q of 10.6 against 418 pH and 10.9 from EM.

![The tank coil from EM (dots) and from its snp2le model in VACASK's ACSP (lines): differential inductance and Q, reflection and transmission.](fig/vco_top/vco_ind_tb_acsp_vacask.svg){#fig-vco-ind-acsp}

::: {.callout-note}
The substrate network of the coil model returns to the global ground node `0`, so `VSS` has to be the ground of every testbench that uses it.
:::

## Circuit Simulation with Xschem and VACASK {#sec-rf-sim}

### Why VACASK

[VACASK](https://codeberg.org/arpadbuermen/VACASK) by Árpád Bűrmen is a circuit simulator with a Spectre-like netlist syntax, whose device models are Verilog-A compiled with OpenVAF. The IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container ships it with the complete set of RF analyses since its `2026.10` release: ACSP, transient noise, HB, HBAC, HBNOISE, PSS, PAC and PNOISE. ngspice, the other simulator of the flow, has an S-parameter analysis and transient noise, but no periodic small-signal or noise analysis in its releases. The `vco` therefore uses both simulators: ngspice for the transients (start-up, corners, power-up, post-layout), VACASK for everything that needs the periodic steady state and for the transient noise. Two simulators that share no solver code also check each other: the tuning transient of VACASK agrees with the transient of ngspice within 0.1 % in frequency.

Xschem netlists a testbench for VACASK in the Spectre format. The Makefile picks the simulator from the name of the testbench:

```sh
make sim-xschem                              # vco_top_tb_tran, ngspice
make sim-xschem TB=vco_top_tb_pss_vacask     # oscillator PSS, PNOISE and PAC, VACASK
make sim-xschem TB=vco_top_tb_tune_vacask    # tuning curve, one transient per tuning voltage, VACASK
make sim-xschem TB=vco_ind_tb_acsp_vacask    # S-parameters of the coil model, VACASK
make sim-all                                 # the testbenches of vco_top in sequence
make sim-view-xschem                         # plot what they wrote
```

A name with `_vacask` is netlisted with `xschem set netlist_type spectre` and run with VACASK, any other name with `ngspice -b`. Both write their results as text tables to `testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/data/`: ngspice with `wrdata`, VACASK with a postprocess hook at the end of its control block that converts every rawfile ([`vacask2data.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/vacask2data.py)). The plot scripts read both the same way.

### Large-Signal Analyses

An oscillator has no input, and its DC operating point is the unstable solution it leaves at start-up. Everything that describes it, the frequency, the amplitude, the phase noise and the tuning gain, belongs to its large periodic solution, so an AC or noise analysis at the DC operating point says nothing about it. The RF analyses work in two steps instead:

1. **Large-signal step.** The periodic steady state is computed directly, either in the time domain by shooting (PSS) or in the frequency domain by harmonic balance (HB), without simulating the start-up.
2. **Small-signal step.** The circuit is linearized around that periodic solution, which gives a linear periodically time-varying system. PAC and HBAC compute its transfer from one sideband to another, PNOISE and HBNOISE its noise with all the noise folded in from the harmonics.

Transient noise is the exception: it injects random noise into an ordinary transient without any linearization, and shares no code with the periodic analyses, which makes it their independent cross-check (@sec-rf-trannoise).

| Analysis | What it computes | In the `vco` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `tran` | transient | start-up (`vco_top_tb_tran`), tuning curve (`vco_top_tb_tune_vacask`), corners, power-up and post-layout |
| `acsp` | S-parameters from an AC analysis with ports | the coil model against its EM data (`vco_ind_tb_acsp_vacask`) |
| `pss` | periodic steady state by shooting, for an oscillator with the period as an unknown (`oscillator=1`) | frequency, waveform and output power (`vco_top_tb_pss_vacask`, post-layout `vco_top_tb_pss_lpe_vacask`) |
| `pac` | small-signal transfer around the PSS, sideband to sideband | the tuning gain $K_\mathrm{VCO}$ from a small tone on `vtune` |
| `pnoise` | noise around the PSS, modulated and folded | the phase noise and its contributions |
| transient noise | `tran` with random noise sources | the phase noise of the schematic against PNOISE, and of the post-layout netlist (`vco_top_tb_trannoise_vacask`, `vco_top_tb_trannoise_lpe_vacask`) |
| `hb` | periodic or multi-tone steady state by harmonic balance | not used, it suits driven circuits such as the buffer, mixers and detectors |
| `hbac`, `hbnoise` | small-signal transfer and noise around the HB solution | not used, the HB counterparts of `pac` and `pnoise` |

: VACASK analyses and where the `vco` uses them. {#tbl-rf-analyses tbl-colwidths="[15,45,40]"}

::: {.callout-tip}
## RF Circuit Simulation in the RFIC Course
The appendix [RF Circuit Simulation](https://iic-jku.github.io/radio-frequency-integrated-circuits/rfic.html#sec-simulation) of the JKU course Radio-Frequency Integrated Circuits explains every analysis of @tbl-rf-analyses, from the DC operating point to PNOISE and HBNOISE, shows how to check their results against each other, and recommends analyses for LNAs, mixers, oscillators, switched-capacitor circuits, power detectors and power amplifiers. SPARX uses HB, HBAC, HBNOISE and transient noise on its 160 GHz power detector and checks them against PSS, PAC and PNOISE, see the [Circuit Simulation](https://iic-jku.github.io/SG13CMOS_SPARX/#sec-sim) chapter of its documentation.
:::

### Anatomy of the PSS Testbench {#sec-rf-tb-pss}

@fig-vco-tb-pss shows `vco_top_tb_pss_vacask`. The macro drives an AC-coupled 50 $\Omega$ load per output, and the sources set the supply, the enable and the tuning voltage. The analyses are in the VACASK control block, here without its comments:

```text
control
  abort always
  var vdd=1.5
  options strictsave=1 pss_minpts=8000 reltol=3e-5
  save v(vout_p) v(vout_n) v("x1:rf_p") v("x1:rf_n")
  save dv(vout_p) dv(vout_n) dv("x1:rf_p") dv("x1:rf_n")
  analysis pss pss oscillator=1 tper=44.3p tstab=12n stabstep=0.5p maxharm=20 ic={"x1:rf_p", 0.8, "x1:rf_n", 0.7} store="osc"
  options strictsave=1 pss_minpts=8000 reltol=3e-5 tran_fbr=0.02 relrefres="pointglobal"
  analysis pnoise pnoise psssolve=0 ic="osc" truncharm=20 in="Vtune" out=["vout_p", "vout_n"] outharm=1 from=10k to=100M mode="dec" points=10
  analysis pac pac psssolve=0 ic="osc" truncharm=20 outharm=1 from=10k to=100M mode="dec" points=10
  postprocess(PYTHON, "../plot_simulations/vacask2data.py", "vco_top_tb_pss_vacask")
endc
```

![Xschem testbench `vco_top_tb_pss_vacask` with its VACASK control block.](fig/vco_top/vco_top_tb_pss_vacask_schematic.svg){#fig-vco-tb-pss}

- **`abort always`** stops VACASK with a nonzero exit code when an analysis fails. Without it, VACASK exits 0 and the plot scripts read the rawfiles of the previous run.
- **`pss oscillator=1`** solves for the period as well, with `tper` as the guess. The initial condition `ic` kicks the tank away from its symmetric operating point, and the stabilization transient `tstab` lets the oscillation build up before the shooting Newton starts. `stabstep` limits its first time step. `store="osc"` keeps the solution for the analyses that follow.
- **`pss_minpts=8000`** gives the shooting at least 8000 time steps per period. At the default 1000 its Newton iteration cycles without converging, and at 4000 it can settle on a period that reads false noise on one buffer device, 4 dB too much at 1 MHz, without an error.
- **`reltol=3e-5`** is for the bias filters of the buffer. Their time constant is 1 $\mu$s against a 44 ps period, so they barely move over one period, and at the default tolerance the shooting settled them 70 mV away from their DC values without an error.
- **`pnoise` and `pac`** start from the stored solution (`psssolve=0 ic="osc"`) and observe the first harmonic at the outputs (`outharm=1`). `pac` drives the small-signal tone of the source `Vtune` (`smag=1`, 1 V) and observes the sideband it modulates onto the carrier, from which the plot script computes the tuning gain.
- **`tran_fbr=0.02`** works around a VACASK bug that is fixed in its sources since commit `7c38094` (November 2026): the period that `pnoise` and `pac` integrate restarts with a backward-Euler step at every sample, which reads the phase noise and the tuning gain low at small offsets, here the phase noise by 3.3 dB at 1 MHz. **`relrefres="pointglobal"`** takes the residual reference of the Newton from the largest contribution at the time point, since the RF decaps `Cg1` and `Cg2` on the static `vbg_buf` make the reference of that node so small that the check fails on residuals of 1e-18. The options are global, so the second `options` line restates the others.

::: {.callout-warning}
## PSS Does Not Prove Start-Up
A PSS finds a periodic solution, but it does not show that the oscillator reaches it after power-up. The start-up is checked with transients, at every corner (@sec-rf-corners) and from the supply ramp (@sec-rf-powerup). And a PSS can settle a slow state wrongly without an error, so [`plot_vco_top.py`](https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13g2-ams-chip-template/blob/main/macros/vco/testbenches/xschem/plot_simulations/plot_vco_top.py) compares its frequency with the tuning transient at the same tuning voltage and warns above 0.3 %.
:::

### Results

The start-up transient of @fig-vco-tran reaches its full amplitude within a few periods of the kick and oscillates at 22.51 GHz, with the tank nodes swinging from 0.10 V to 1.53 V. The PSS of @fig-vco-pss agrees on the frequency within 0.2 % and gives the output power at the fundamental, -8.3 dBm per output.

![Start-up transient of the schematic (ngspice): the differential tank voltage, and the last 200 ps of the tank nodes and the differential output.](fig/vco_top/vco_top_tb_tran.svg){#fig-vco-tran}

![Oscillator PSS (VACASK): one period of the tank and the outputs, and the spectrum of the output.](fig/vco_top/vco_top_tb_pss_vacask_pss.svg){#fig-vco-pss}

The spectrum in @fig-vco-pss is that of one output. Its harmonics come from the buffer, a differential pair driven by the tank's full swing into resistive loads, and not from the tank.
